The Minimum Subpacketization of Reed-Solomon Codes with Linear Repair Achieving the Cut-Set Bound

Weijun Fang    Jing Qiu    Shu-Tao Xia    Fang-Wei Fu ††thanks: This work was supported in part by the National Key Research and Development Program of China under Grants 2022YFA1004900 and 2022YFA1005000; by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grants 62571298, 62571301, and 62371259; by the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities of China (Nankai University); by the Nankai Zhide Foundation; and by the China Postdoctoral Science Foundation under Grant 2025M773088. (Corresponding author: Jing Qiu.)††thanks: Weijun Fang is with the State Key Laboratory of Cryptography and Digital Economy Security, the Key Laboratory of Cryptologic Technology and Information Security, Ministry of Education, and the School of Cyber Science and Technology, Shandong University, Qingdao 266237, China (e-mail: fwj@sdu.edu.cn).††thanks: Jing Qiu and Shu-Tao Xia are with the Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University, Shenzhen, Guangdong 518055, China (e-mails: {jing_qiu, xiast}@sz.tsinghua.edu.cn).††thanks: Fang-Wei Fu is with the Chern Institute of Mathematics and LPMC, Nankai University, Tianjin 300071, China (e-mail: fwfu@nankai.edu.cn).
Abstract

In this paper, we study the minimum subpacketization of (n,k)(n,k) Reed-Solomon (RS) codes over 𝔽qℓ\mathbb{F}_{q^{\ell}} admitting cut-set-optimal exact 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear repair of every coordinate from any dd helpers. For 3≤k<d≤n−13\leq k<d\leq n-1, write s=d+1−ks=d+1-k and denote this minimum by ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q). Using divisibility and relative-degree constraints on cross-ratio fields of evaluation sets, we establish ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≥s​Gs​(d+1)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\geq sG_{s}(d+1), where Gs​(m)G_{s}(m) is the minimum product of mm pairwise coprime integers, each at least ss. Let Δs​(n,d)\Delta_{s}(n,d) be the minimum of lcm⁡(a1,…,an)\operatorname{lcm}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}) over positive integers a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n} satisfying lcm(aj:j∈J∪{i})≥slcm(aj:j∈J)\operatorname{lcm}(a_{j}:j\in J\cup\{i\})\geq s\operatorname{lcm}(a_{j}:j\in J) for every dd-subset J⊆[n]J\subseteq[n] and every i∈[n]∖Ji\in[n]\setminus J. We construct RS codes with subpacketization s​Δs​(n,d)s\Delta_{s}(n,d) and further prove that ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=s​Δs​(n,d)=s​Gs​(n)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=s\Delta_{s}(n,d)=sG_{s}(n) whenever d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1), for every prime power qq. In particular, this determines the minimum subpacketization in the full-helper case d=n−1d=n-1, resolving the corresponding exact linear-repair case of Open Problem 20 posed by Ramkumar et al. in their survey on codes for distributed storage. We further give a finite formula for Gs​(n)G_{s}(n) and determine the exact threshold for its closed-form expression in terms of the first nn primes. For fixed kk and dd, we prove log⁡ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=Θk,d​(log⁡n​log⁡log⁡n)\log\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=\Theta_{k,d}(\log n\log\log n) as n→∞n\to\infty, using divisor-function estimates and cover-free families. An affine-plane construction shows that Δs​(n,d)<Gs​(n)\Delta_{s}(n,d)<G_{s}(n) for some parameters, so s​Gs​(n)sG_{s}(n) is not a universal formula. We conjecture that ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=s​Δs​(n,d)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=s\Delta_{s}(n,d) for every prime power qq and all 3≤k<d≤n−13\leq k<d\leq n-1.

Index Terms: 
Reed-Solomon codes, linear repair, cut-set bound, subpacketization, cross-ratios.

I Introduction

Scalar maximum-distance-separable (MDS) codes are a basic model for storage-optimal erasure protection. An (n,k)(n,k) scalar MDS code over a field KK stores one KK-symbol in each of nn nodes and allows the original kk information symbols to be recovered from any kk nodes. Equivalently, it tolerates any n−kn-k node erasures with the minimum possible redundancy. This global recovery property, however, does not ensure communication-efficient repair of an individual failed node. A direct repair procedure downloads one complete KK-symbol from each of kk surviving nodes and reconstructs the entire codeword, even though only one symbol is missing.

This inefficiency motivates the array-code viewpoint. In an MDS array code over a base field FF, each node stores a vector of ℓ\ell subsymbols, and a helper may transmit functions of its stored vector rather than its entire contents. The regenerating-code framework of Dimakis et al. [1] formalizes the resulting tradeoff between storage and repair communication. If a failed node is repaired from dd helpers and γ\gamma denotes the total number of downloaded FF-symbols, then every MDS array code satisfies the cut-set bound

γ≥d​ℓd+1−k.\gamma\geq\frac{d\ell}{d+1-k}. (1)

An MDS array code attaining equality in (1) is a minimum-storage regenerating (MSR) code. Much of the literature on exact-repair MSR codes has focused on MDS array codes; representative constructions include the product-matrix construction [2] and high-rate constructions with optimal repair bandwidth [3]. The node size ℓ\ell, called the subpacketization, determines the granularity available to a repair scheme and is a principal measure of its algebraic and implementation complexity. Fundamental lower bounds on the subpacketization of MSR array codes were developed in [4, 5, 6]. On the construction side, Liu, Li, and Tang constructed high-rate optimal-access MSR codes over small finite fields [7], while Li, Tang, and Tian developed a generic transformation that, when applied iteratively, enables optimal repair of all nodes with controlled subpacketization [8]. Liu, Li, and Tang later extended this line to MDS array codes supporting multiple repair degrees, with smaller subpacketization than earlier multi-degree constructions [9]. More recently, Wang, Li, Hu, and Ye constructed MSR codes with d=k+1d=k+1 and subpacketization 2⌈n/3⌉2^{\lceil n/3\rceil} while maintaining a field size linear in nn [10]. With s=d+1−ks=d+1-k, Li, Wang, Hu, and Ye subsequently gave, for every admissible repair degree, optimal-access MSR codes over fields of size Os​(n)O_{s}(n) with subpacketization ℓ=s⌈n/s⌉\ell=s^{\lceil n/s\rceil} and also non-optimal-access MSR codes with the smaller subpacketization s⌈n/(s+1)⌉s^{\lceil n/(s+1)\rceil} [11]. These developments highlight the central role of subpacketization in general MSR array-code design and motivate the corresponding minimum subpacketization problem for the much more rigid class of scalar Reed-Solomon codes.

Reed-Solomon (RS) codes [12] are one of the most important families of scalar MDS codes and are widely used in communication and storage systems. Let F=𝔽qF=\mathbb{F}_{q} and K=𝔽qℓK=\mathbb{F}_{q^{\ell}}. Although an RS code is a scalar code over KK, after fixing an FF-basis of KK, each symbol in KK can be represented as a vector in FℓF^{\ell}. Thus, the same code can be viewed as an MDS array code over FF with subpacketization ℓ\ell. This scalar-to-array viewpoint has also been used more generally in the repair of scalar MDS codes [13].

This viewpoint allows the repair of RS codes to be studied within the regenerating-code framework. However, unlike unrestricted MDS array codes, RS codes are subject to additional algebraic constraints arising from their scalar extension field and polynomial-evaluation structure. Consequently, the repair bandwidth and subpacketization of RS codes have attracted substantial attention. In this paper, we require exact FF-linear repair of every coordinate from every set of dd helper nodes with bandwidth meeting the cut-set bound in (1), and seek the minimum possible extension degree ℓ=[K:F]\ell=[K:F].

I-A Linear Repair of Reed-Solomon Codes

The systematic study of bandwidth-efficient linear repair of scalar RS codes was initiated by Guruswami and Wootters [14]. They established a dual-code characterization of exact FF-linear repair, reducing the design of a repair scheme to the construction of suitable collections of dual codewords, and used trace maps to obtain nontrivial repair schemes for full-length RS codes. Building on this framework, Dau and Milenkovic [15], and later Dau et al. [16], developed optimal repair schemes for additional families of full-length RS codes, including constructions based on subspace polynomials. Here optimality refers to their full-length families and specified redundancy ranges under their linear-repair lower bounds; it need not mean equality in (1). Li, Wang, and Jafarkhani [17] further investigated explicit tradeoffs between repair bandwidth and subpacketization.

A major breakthrough was achieved by Tamo, Ye, and Barg [18, 19], who constructed RS codes attaining the cut-set bound for the repair of any single failed node from any prescribed set of dd helper nodes. With s=d+1−ks=d+1-k, the subpacketization of their construction is

ℓ=s​∏i=1np~i,\ell=s\prod_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{p}_{i},

where p~1,…,p~n\tilde{p}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{p}_{n} are distinct primes satisfying p~i≡1(mods)\tilde{p}_{i}\equiv 1\pmod{s}. Their framework also extends to multiple erasures. Subsequent work developed optimal-access and error-resilient repair schemes [20], while near-optimal repair bandwidth with substantially smaller subpacketization was studied in [21].

In our prior work [22], we developed a basis-transformation method for constructing the required repair subspaces for every integer relative extension degree p≥sp\geq s, without the congruence restriction p≡1(mods)p\equiv 1\pmod{s}. Applying this method to the Tamo-Ye-Barg framework, we obtained RS codes attaining the cut-set bound using arbitrary distinct prime degrees pi≥sp_{i}\geq s.

These constructions establish the existence of cut-set-optimal RS repair schemes, but do not determine the least possible subpacketization: assigning distinct prime degrees is only one way to meet the repair requirements. The present paper studies the minimum over all RS evaluation sets, allowing more general degree assignments and deriving lower bounds that apply to every such code.

I-B Main Results

For a prime power qq and integers 3≤k<d≤n−13\leq k<d\leq n-1, let ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q) denote the smallest integer ℓ\ell for which an (n,k)(n,k) RS code over 𝔽qℓ\mathbb{F}_{q^{\ell}} admits cut-set-optimal exact 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear repair of every coordinate from every dd-helper set. Write s=d+1−k≥2s=d+1-k\geq 2.

Our results are expressed in terms of two arithmetic quantities. For m≥1m\geq 1, define

Gs(m)=min{∏i=1mgi:gi∈ℤ,gi≥s,gcd(gi,gj)=1 for i≠j},G_{s}(m)=\min\left\{\prod_{i=1}^{m}g_{i}:g_{i}\in\mathbb{Z},\ g_{i}\geq s,\ \gcd(g_{i},g_{j})=1\text{ for }i\neq j\right\},

with Gs​(0)=1G_{s}(0)=1. For 1≤t<N1\leq t<N, let Δs​(N,t)\Delta_{s}(N,t) be the minimum of lcm⁡(a1,…,aN)\operatorname{lcm}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}) over positive integers a1,…,aNa_{1},\ldots,a_{N} satisfying

lcm(aj:j∈J∪{i})≥slcm(aj:j∈J)\operatorname{lcm}(a_{j}:j\in J\cup\{i\})\geq s\,\operatorname{lcm}(a_{j}:j\in J) (2)

for every i∈[N]i\in[N] and every tt-subset J⊆[N]∖{i}J\subseteq[N]\setminus\{i\}. The first quantity minimizes a product of pairwise coprime degrees; the second permits shared factors, subject to the relative-degree requirement imposed by every failed-coordinate/helper-set pair. In particular, Δs​(n,d)≤Gs​(n)\Delta_{s}(n,d)\leq G_{s}(n).

Our principal result determines the minimum subpacketization exactly. For every prime power qq and all 3≤k<d≤n−13\leq k<d\leq n-1 satisfying d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1), or equivalently d≥4​n+5−1d\geq\sqrt{4n+5}-1, we prove

ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=s​Δs​(n,d)=s​Gs​(n).\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=s\Delta_{s}(n,d)=sG_{s}(n). (3)

Thus the exact formula applies even when the number of helpers is of order n\sqrt{n}. For full-helper repair (d=n−1d=n-1), this yields

ℓmin​(n,k,n−1,q)=(n−k)​Gn−k​(n),3≤k<n−1.\ell_{\min}(n,k,n-1;q)=(n-k)G_{n-k}(n),\qquad 3\leq k<n-1.

This settles the exact 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear repair case, in the stated dimension range, of Open Problem 20 posed by Ramkumar et al. [23, Open Problem 20].

The main ingredients of the proof and our further contributions are as follows.

  1. 1.

    Our lower bounds come from the divisibility and relative-degree constraints imposed by cut-set-optimal repair on the fields generated by projective cross-ratios of the evaluation points. Applying these constraints to a punctured (d+1,k)(d+1,k) RS code in which every coordinate admits cut-set-optimal full-helper repair yields

    ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≥s​Gs​(d+1),\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\geq sG_{s}(d+1),

    which strengthens the lower bound of Tamo, Ye, and Barg [18, Theorem 5] for scalar MDS codes when specialized to RS codes. By using the constraints from all failed-coordinate/helper-set pairs, we first establish ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≥s​Δs​(n,d)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\geq s\Delta_{s}(n,d) for 2​d≥n+32d\geq n+3. To go beyond this range, we combine compositum identities for cross-ratio fields with a finer analysis of the private and shared prime factors of their degrees. Consequently, we establish ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≥s​Gs​(n)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\geq sG_{s}(n) whenever d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1).

  2. 2.

    For the matching upper bound, we extend the distinct-prime constructions to general feasible degree assignments. Our prior work [22, Theorem 3] provides the necessary repair-subspace decomposition for every integer relative degree p≥sp\geq s. We show that every tuple satisfying (2) with (N,t)=(n,d)(N,t)=(n,d) yields an RS code with subpacketization s​lcm⁡(a1,…,an)s\operatorname{lcm}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}) that achieves the cut-set bound for every repair configuration. Unlike the earlier constructions with pairwise distinct prime degrees, these tuples may contain composite degrees with shared prime factors. Minimizing over all feasible tuples, we obtain

    ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≤s​Δs​(n,d)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\leq s\Delta_{s}(n,d)

    for every admissible parameter set and every prime power qq. Together with the lower bounds, this proves (3).

  3. 3.

    We also study the arithmetic quantity Gs​(m)G_{s}(m) appearing in the exact formula. In addition to a finite formula valid for all mm, we determine the exact threshold for the closed-form expression given below. Let pjp_{j} denote the jj-th prime, and write pm#=∏j=1mpjp_{m}^{\#}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}p_{j} for m≥1m\geq 1, with p0#=1p_{0}^{\#}=1. Also put As=lcm⁡(1,…,s−1)A_{s}=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,s-1). For s≥3s\geq 3, let usu_{s} and vsv_{s} be the largest prime and the largest prime power, respectively, strictly below ss, and set u2=v2=1u_{2}=v_{2}=1. Then

    Gs(m)=Aspm#⟺m≥π(usvs),G_{s}(m)=A_{s}p_{m}^{\#}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m\geq\pi(u_{s}v_{s}),

    where π⁡(x)\pi(x) counts the primes at most xx. In particular, G2​(m)=pm#G_{2}(m)=p_{m}^{\#} for every mm, giving an explicit expression for (3) when s=2s=2.

  4. 4.

    For fixed kk and dd (and any fixed prime power qq), we further prove

    log⁡ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=Θk,d​(log⁡n​log⁡log⁡n)(n→∞).\log\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=\Theta_{k,d}(\log n\log\log n)\qquad(n\to\infty).

    The lower bound has leading coefficient (d−3)/log⁡2(d-3)/\log 2, and the matching-order upper bound follows from cover-free families and our degree construction. By comparison, for fixed ss, the earlier constructions using the smallest admissible distinct prime degrees satisfy log⁡ℓ=Θ⁡(n​log⁡n)\log\ell=\Theta(n\log n).

Finally, the equality ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=s​Gs​(n)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=sG_{s}(n) does not hold for all admissible parameters. An affine-plane construction in Appendix B exhibits parameters for which Δs​(n,d)<Gs​(n)\Delta_{s}(n,d)<G_{s}(n) and hence ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)<s​Gs​(n)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)<sG_{s}(n). This distinction suggests that Δs​(n,d)\Delta_{s}(n,d), rather than Gs​(n)G_{s}(n), governs the general problem. We conjecture that

ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=s​Δs​(n,d)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=s\Delta_{s}(n,d)

for every prime power qq and all 3≤k<d≤n−13\leq k<d\leq n-1.

I-C Organization

Section II reviews linear repair and the basis-transformation result used in our construction. Section III develops the cross-ratio constraints and proves the general and parameter-dependent lower bounds. Section IV constructs RS codes from feasible degree tuples, establishes (3), and derives exact formulas for Gs​(m)G_{s}(m). Section V determines the fixed-parameter asymptotic order of the minimum subpacketization. The appendices give auxiliary prime-product estimates and an affine-plane construction exhibiting Δs​(n,d)<Gs​(n)\Delta_{s}(n,d)<G_{s}(n).

II Preliminaries

We write ℤ\mathbb{Z} for the integers and [m]={1,…,m}[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\} for any positive integer mm. All logarithms without an explicitly indicated base are natural. Table I summarizes the principal notation; symbols specific to individual arguments are defined where needed.

II-A Reed-Solomon Codes and Linear Repair

Throughout, let F=𝔽q⊆K=𝔽qℓF=\mathbb{F}_{q}\subseteq K=\mathbb{F}_{q^{\ell}} and let α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n} be pairwise distinct elements of KK, and put Ω={α1,…,αn}\Omega=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\}. The Reed-Solomon code with evaluation set Ω\Omega is defined as

C=RSK(n,k,Ω)={(f(α1),…,f(αn)):f∈K[x],degf<k}.C=\operatorname{RS}_{K}(n,k,\Omega)=\left\{(f(\alpha_{1}),\ldots,f(\alpha_{n})):f\in K[x],\ \deg f<k\right\}.

Its Euclidean dual, with respect to the inner product ∑j=1nxj​yj\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}y_{j}, is the generalized RS code

C⟂={(w1g(α1),…,wng(αn)):g∈K[x],degg<n−k},C^{\perp}=\left\{(w_{1}g(\alpha_{1}),\ldots,w_{n}g(\alpha_{n})):g\in K[x],\ \deg g<n-k\right\},

where wj=∏t≠j(αj−αt)−1w_{j}=\prod_{t\neq j}(\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{t})^{-1}.

Viewing KK as an ℓ\ell-dimensional vector space over FF turns each code coordinate into a node containing ℓ\ell FF-symbols. An FF-linear repair scheme for a failed coordinate ii downloads FF-linear functionals of the symbols stored in a helper set H⊆[n]∖{i}H\subseteq[n]\setminus\{i\} and reconstructs the missing element of KK. For |H|=d|H|=d, put

s=d+1−k.s=d+1-k.

The cut-set bound requires any exact repair scheme to download at least d​ℓ/sd\ell/s FF-symbols in total. We call a repair scheme cut-set optimal if equality holds. Throughout, we require cut-set-optimal FF-linear repair of every coordinate from every dd-helper set.

We use the following dual-code characterization of linear repair from [14, Theorem 4].

Theorem 1 ([14, Theorem 4]).

Let C⊆KnC\subseteq K^{n} be a scalar linear MDS code with [K:F]=ℓ[K:F]=\ell, and fix i∈[n]i\in[n]. Then coordinate ii admits exact FF-linear repair from the other n−1n-1 coordinates with bandwidth at most bb if and only if there exist ℓ\ell codewords 𝐩(1),…,𝐩(ℓ)∈C⟂\bm{p}^{(1)},\ldots,\bm{p}^{(\ell)}\in C^{\perp} such that

dimFSpanF⁡{pi(t):1≤t≤ℓ}=ℓ\dim_{F}\operatorname{Span}_{F}\{p_{i}^{(t)}:1\leq t\leq\ell\}=\ell

and

∑j≠idimFSpanF⁡{pj(t):1≤t≤ℓ}≤b.\sum_{j\neq i}\dim_{F}\operatorname{Span}_{F}\{p_{j}^{(t)}:1\leq t\leq\ell\}\leq b.

In particular, in the full-helper case d=n−1d=n-1, if the repair is cut-set optimal and s=n−ks=n-k, then the codewords in Theorem 1 satisfy

SpanF⁡{pi(t):1≤t≤ℓ}=K\operatorname{Span}_{F}\{p_{i}^{(t)}:1\leq t\leq\ell\}=K

and

∑j≠idimFSpanF⁡{pj(t):1≤t≤ℓ}=(n−1)​ℓs.\sum_{j\neq i}\dim_{F}\operatorname{Span}_{F}\{p_{j}^{(t)}:1\leq t\leq\ell\}=\frac{(n-1)\ell}{s}.
Remark 1.

A simple but useful consequence is the following. If coordinate ii admits cut-set-optimal repair from a dd-helper set HH, then puncturing all coordinates outside H∪{i}H\cup\{i\} yields a length-(d+1)(d+1) MDS code with cut-set-optimal full-helper repair of the same coordinate. The parameter s=d+1−ks=d+1-k remains unchanged. This reduction allows us to focus on full-helper repair in many of the subsequent lower-bound arguments.

As in the Introduction, ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q) denotes the minimum subpacketization for cut-set-optimal FF-linear repair of every coordinate from every dd-helper set. Coordinate permutations and nonzero coordinate scalings preserve FF-linear repair bandwidth. Consequently, a generalized RS code and the ordinary RS code obtained by removing its coordinate multipliers are equivalent for the present purpose.

II-B Finite-Field Degrees and Local Repair Subspaces

Let F¯\overline{F} be an algebraic closure of FF. For x1,…,xt∈F¯x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}\in\overline{F} and every nonempty I⊆[t]I\subseteq[t], the finite-field compositum formula [24, Chapter 2] gives

[F(xi:i∈I):F]=lcm([F(xi):F]:i∈I).[F(x_{i}:i\in I):F]=\operatorname{lcm}([F(x_{i}):F]:i\in I).

In particular,

𝔽qa​𝔽qb=𝔽qlcm⁡(a,b).\mathbb{F}_{q^{a}}\mathbb{F}_{q^{b}}=\mathbb{F}_{q^{\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)}}.

For a finite extension K/LK/L and x∈Kx\in K, write

TrK/L(x)=∑j=0[K:L]−1x|L|j.\operatorname{Tr}_{K/L}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{[K:L]-1}x^{|L|^{j}}.

Finite-field extensions are separable, so the pairing K×K⟶LK\times K\longrightarrow L, (x,y)↦TrK/L⁡(x​y)(x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_{K/L}(xy), is nondegenerate [24, Chapter 2].

In the construction of Tamo, Ye, and Barg [19], the evaluation points are assigned distinct prime degrees p~i\tilde{p}_{i} satisfying

p~i≡1(mods).\tilde{p}_{i}\equiv 1\pmod{s}.

This congruence condition is used in constructing the local repair-enabling subspaces and restricts the available degree choices.

Our prior work [22, Theorem 3] removed this restriction by a basis-transformation argument and established the following subspace decomposition for every integer relative degree r≥sr\geq s.

Theorem 2 ([22, Theorem 3]).

Let F0⊂E0=F0​(α)⊂K0F_{0}\subset E_{0}=F_{0}(\alpha)\subset K_{0} be finite fields with

[E0:F0]=r≥s=[K0:E0].[E_{0}:F_{0}]=r\geq s=[K_{0}:E_{0}].

Then there exists an explicitly constructible F0F_{0}-subspace S0⊆K0S_{0}\subseteq K_{0} satisfying

dimF0S0=r,K0=⨁u=0s−1αu​S0.\dim_{F_{0}}S_{0}=r,\qquad K_{0}=\bigoplus_{u=0}^{s-1}\alpha^{u}S_{0}.

In Section IV, this result will be applied with the relative extension degree of a failed evaluation point over the field generated by the chosen helpers.

III Lower Bounds on Subpacketization

In this section, we establish lower bounds on the subpacketization. We first translate cut-set-optimal repair into degree constraints on cross-ratio fields. Applying these constraints to a punctured (d+1,k)(d+1,k) RS code yields a lower bound valid for all admissible parameters. We then combine the constraints from all helper sets. For 2​d≥n+32d\geq n+3, we obtain the lower bound s​Δs​(n,d)s\Delta_{s}(n,d). Finally, a more detailed analysis of the same degree system yields the stronger bound s​Gs​(n)sG_{s}(n) whenever d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1).

III-A Cross-Ratio Constraints

We begin with the full-helper case, which will later be applied to a failed coordinate together with a chosen helper set. Throughout this subsection, assume

d=n−1,k≥3,s=n−k≥2,d=n-1,\qquad k\geq 3,\qquad s=n-k\geq 2,

and write

C=RSK⁡(n,k,Ω),Ω={α1,…,αn}.C=\operatorname{RS}_{K}(n,k,\Omega),\qquad\Omega=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\}.

Fix i∈[n]i\in[n] and consider cut-set-optimal FF-linear repair of coordinate ii. We write K​[x]<sK[x]_{<s} for the space of polynomials over KK of degree less than ss, including the zero polynomial. The following lemma records the dimension properties of the evaluation spaces that follow from equality in the cut-set bound. The underlying argument is essentially the one used by Tamo, Ye, and Barg [18, proof of Theorem 5]; we state it in the polynomial form needed below. See also [19].

Lemma 1.

Suppose that the failed coordinate i∈[n]i\in[n], with evaluation point αi\alpha_{i}, admits cut-set-optimal FF-linear repair from the other n−1n-1 coordinates. Then s|ℓs\mid\ell, and there exists an ℓ\ell-dimensional FF-subspace 𝒫i⊆K​[x]<s\mathcal{P}_{i}\subseteq K[x]_{<s} whose evaluation spaces, defined for y∈Ky\in K by

Uy:={f⁡(y):f∈𝒫i},U_{y}:=\{f(y):f\in\mathcal{P}_{i}\},

satisfy Uαi=KU_{\alpha_{i}}=K and

dimFUy=ℓsfor every ​y∈Ω∖{αi}.\dim_{F}U_{y}=\frac{\ell}{s}\quad\text{for every }y\in\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}.

Moreover, for every ss-subset B={b1,…,bs}⊆Ω∖{αi}B=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{s}\}\subseteq\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\} and every choice of au∈Ubua_{u}\in U_{b_{u}}, 1≤u≤s1\leq u\leq s, there is an f∈𝒫if\in\mathcal{P}_{i} such that f⁡(bu)=auf(b_{u})=a_{u} for all uu.

Proof.

By Theorem 1 and the dual form of RS codes, choose polynomials f1,…,fℓ∈K​[x]<sf_{1},\ldots,f_{\ell}\in K[x]_{<s} whose values at αi\alpha_{i} form an FF-basis of KK and whose helper evaluation spans have total dimension at most (n−1)​ℓ/s(n-1)\ell/s. Nonzero dual multipliers do not change these dimensions. Set

𝒫i=SpanF⁡{f1,…,fℓ}.\mathcal{P}_{i}=\operatorname{Span}_{F}\{f_{1},\ldots,f_{\ell}\}.

Then dimF𝒫i=ℓ\dim_{F}\mathcal{P}_{i}=\ell and Uαi=KU_{\alpha_{i}}=K.

For each helper point y∈Ω∖{αi}y\in\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}, put

ty=dimFUy.t_{y}=\dim_{F}U_{y}.

The selected polynomials yield a repair scheme with bandwidth ∑yty\sum_{y}t_{y}. The preceding upper bound and the cut-set bound therefore force

∑y∈Ω∖{αi}ty=(n−1)​ℓs.\sum_{y\in\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}}t_{y}=\frac{(n-1)\ell}{s}.

Let BB be any ss-subset of the helper points. A polynomial of degree less than ss is determined by its values on BB, so evaluation on BB is injective on 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}. Its image has dimension ℓ\ell and is contained in the space of all tuples with values in UyU_{y} at each y∈By\in B. Hence

ℓ≤∑y∈Bty.\ell\leq\sum_{y\in B}t_{y}. (4)

Summing the nonnegative differences over all such BB gives

∑B⊆Ω∖{αi}|B|=s(∑y∈Bty−ℓ)=(n−2s−1)​(n−1)​ℓs−(n−1s)​ℓ=0.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}B\subseteq\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}\\ |B|=s\end{subarray}}\left(\sum_{y\in B}t_{y}-\ell\right)=\binom{n-2}{s-1}\frac{(n-1)\ell}{s}-\binom{n-1}{s}\ell=0.

Thus ∑y∈Bty=ℓ\sum_{y\in B}t_{y}=\ell for every BB.

Given distinct helper points y,y′y,y^{\prime}, choose an (s−1)(s-1)-subset B′B^{\prime} of the remaining helper points; this is possible since n−3≥s−1n-3\geq s-1. Comparing B′∪{y}B^{\prime}\cup\{y\} and B′∪{y′}B^{\prime}\cup\{y^{\prime}\} shows that ty=ty′t_{y}=t_{y^{\prime}}. The total sum then yields ty=ℓ/st_{y}=\ell/s for every helper point.

Finally, fix B={b1,…,bs}B=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{s}\}. The space of all tuples with entries in the corresponding UbuU_{b_{u}} has dimension ℓ\ell. By injectivity, the evaluation tuples from 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} form a subspace of the same dimension. The two spaces therefore coincide, so every prescribed tuple is attained. ∎

We next derive relations among the helper evaluation spaces. For a field LL, the projective line ℙ1​(L)\mathbb{P}^{1}(L) consists of nonzero vectors in L2L^{2} modulo nonzero scalar multiples. For column vectors u=(u0,u1)𝖳∈L2u=(u_{0},u_{1})^{\mathsf{T}}\in L^{2} and v=(v0,v1)𝖳∈L2v=(v_{0},v_{1})^{\mathsf{T}}\in L^{2}, write

det(u,v):=det[u​v]=u0​v1−u1​v0.\det(u,v):=\det[\,u\ v\,]=u_{0}v_{1}-u_{1}v_{0}.

Here GL2​(L)\mathrm{GL}_{2}(L) is the group of invertible 2×22\times 2 matrices over LL, and PGL2​(L)\mathrm{PGL}_{2}(L) is its quotient by nonzero scalar matrices. For four distinct points x,z,a,b∈ℙ1​(F¯)x,z,a,b\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\overline{F}), choose nonzero column-vector representatives, denoted by the same symbols, and define

χ⁡(x,z,a,b)=det(x,b)​det(z,a)det(x,a)​det(z,b).\chi(x,z;a,b)=\frac{\det(x,b)\det(z,a)}{\det(x,a)\det(z,b)}.

This is independent of the chosen representatives. If T∈PGL2​(F¯)T\in\mathrm{PGL}_{2}(\overline{F}) is induced by A∈GL2​(F¯)A\in\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\overline{F}), then det(A​u,A​v)=det(A)​det(u,v)\det(Au,Av)=\det(A)\det(u,v), and hence

χ⁡(x,z,a,b)=χ⁡(T⁡(x),T⁡(z),T⁡(a),T⁡(b)).\chi(x,z;a,b)=\chi\bigl(T(x),T(z);T(a),T(b)\bigr).

Under the affine chart t↔[t:1]t\leftrightarrow[t:1], with ∞=[1:0]\infty=[1:0], this becomes

χ⁡(x,z,a,b)=(x−b)​(z−a)(x−a)​(z−b)\chi(x,z;a,b)=\frac{(x-b)(z-a)}{(x-a)(z-b)}

when all four points are affine.

Fix an ss-subset B={b1,…,bs}⊆Ω∖{αi}B=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{s}\}\subseteq\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}. For u∈[s]u\in[s], let hu​(x)∈K​[x]<sh_{u}(x)\in K[x]_{<s} be the Lagrange basis polynomial

hu​(x)=∏1≤t≤st≠ux−btbu−bt.h_{u}(x)=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq t\leq s\\ t\neq u\end{subarray}}\frac{x-b_{t}}{b_{u}-b_{t}}.

Fix y∈Ky\in K. For f∈𝒫if\in\mathcal{P}_{i}, f⁡(y)=∑u=1shu​(y)​f​(bu)f(y)=\sum_{u=1}^{s}h_{u}(y)f(b_{u}). By Lemma 1, every tuple of values from the spaces UbuU_{b_{u}} is realized by a polynomial in 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}. Therefore

Uy=∑u=1shu​(y)​Ubu.U_{y}=\sum_{u=1}^{s}h_{u}(y)U_{b_{u}}. (5)

The sum on the right is a sum of FF-subspaces of KK. Here hu​(y)h_{u}(y) is a scalar and

hu​(y)​Ubu={hu​(y)​a:a∈Ubu}h_{u}(y)U_{b_{u}}=\{h_{u}(y)a:a\in U_{b_{u}}\}

is its scalar multiple of the FF-subspace UbuU_{b_{u}}.

At a helper point outside BB, equality of dimensions forces the summands in (5) to coincide. This is the helper-space alignment used in [18, proof of Theorem 5]. Comparing the identities at two helper points yields the following relation.

Lemma 2.

Let B={b1,…,bs}⊆Ω∖{αi}B=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{s}\}\subseteq\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\} and let z∈Ω∖(B∪{αi})z\in\Omega\setminus(B\cup\{\alpha_{i}\}). Then

h1​(z)​Ub1=⋯=hs​(z)​Ubs.h_{1}(z)U_{b_{1}}=\cdots=h_{s}(z)U_{b_{s}}.

Denote this common subspace by A=UzA=U_{z}. For every x∈Ω∖(B∪{αi,z})x\in\Omega\setminus(B\cup\{\alpha_{i},z\}) and every distinct u,v∈[s]u,v\in[s],

χ⁡(x,z,bu,bv)​A=A.\chi(x,z;b_{u},b_{v})A=A. (6)
Proof.

Taking y=zy=z in (5), each nonzero scalar multiple hu​(z)​Ubuh_{u}(z)U_{b_{u}} has dimension ℓ/s\ell/s, while their sum UzU_{z} also has dimension ℓ/s\ell/s. Hence

h1​(z)​Ub1=⋯=hs​(z)​Ubs=Uz=A.h_{1}(z)U_{b_{1}}=\cdots=h_{s}(z)U_{b_{s}}=U_{z}=A.

The same argument at xx yields

hu​(x)​Ubu=hv​(x)​Ubv.h_{u}(x)U_{b_{u}}=h_{v}(x)U_{b_{v}}.

Using hu​(z)​Ubu=hv​(z)​Ubv=Ah_{u}(z)U_{b_{u}}=h_{v}(z)U_{b_{v}}=A, we obtain

hu​(x)​hv​(z)hv​(x)​hu​(z)​A=A.\frac{h_{u}(x)h_{v}(z)}{h_{v}(x)h_{u}(z)}A=A.

A direct calculation using the Lagrange basis shows that

hu​(x)​hv​(z)hv​(x)​hu​(z)=(x−bv)​(z−bu)(x−bu)​(z−bv)=χ⁡(x,z,bu,bv),\frac{h_{u}(x)h_{v}(z)}{h_{v}(x)h_{u}(z)}=\frac{(x-b_{v})(z-b_{u})}{(x-b_{u})(z-b_{v})}=\chi(x,z;b_{u},b_{v}),

which proves (6). ∎

For a finite set X⊆ℙ1​(F¯)X\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{1}(\overline{F}), define

ℛF(X)=F(χ(x,z;a,b):x,z,a,b∈X distinct),\mathscr{R}_{F}(X)=F\bigl(\chi(x,z;a,b):x,z,a,b\in X\text{ distinct}\bigr),

with the convention ℛF​(X)=F\mathscr{R}_{F}(X)=F when |X|≤3|X|\leq 3. We call ℛF​(X)\mathscr{R}_{F}(X) the cross-ratio field of XX over FF.

Fix distinct a,b,c∈ℙ1​(F¯)a,b,c\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\overline{F}). For y∈ℙ1​(F¯)y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\overline{F}), define

ϕa,b,c(y)=[det(y,b)det(c,a):det(y,a)det(c,b)].\phi_{a,b,c}(y)=\bigl[\det(y,b)\det(c,a):\det(y,a)\det(c,b)\bigr].

The two homogeneous coordinate functions are linearly independent linear forms in yy, so ϕa,b,c\phi_{a,b,c} is a projective transformation. It satisfies

ϕa,b,c​(a)=∞,ϕa,b,c​(b)=0,ϕa,b,c​(c)=1.\phi_{a,b,c}(a)=\infty,\qquad\phi_{a,b,c}(b)=0,\qquad\phi_{a,b,c}(c)=1.

For y∉{a,b,c}y\notin\{a,b,c\}, its affine coordinate is

ϕa,b,c​(y)=det(y,b)​det(c,a)det(y,a)​det(c,b)=χ⁡(y,c,a,b).\phi_{a,b,c}(y)=\frac{\det(y,b)\det(c,a)}{\det(y,a)\det(c,b)}=\chi(y,c;a,b). (7)

For y≠ay\neq a, we henceforth also use ϕa,b,c​(y)\phi_{a,b,c}(y) to denote its affine coordinate.

Although the cross-ratio field is defined using all quadruples, it is generated after fixing any three points.

Lemma 3.

Let X⊆ℙ1​(F¯)X\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{1}(\overline{F}) contain distinct points a,b,ca,b,c and write ϕ=ϕa,b,c\phi=\phi_{a,b,c}. Then

ℛF(X)=F(ϕ(y):y∈X∖{a,b,c})=F(χ(y,c;a,b):y∈X∖{a,b,c}).\mathscr{R}_{F}(X)=F\bigl(\phi(y):y\in X\setminus\{a,b,c\}\bigr)=F\bigl(\chi(y,c;a,b):y\in X\setminus\{a,b,c\}\bigr).
Proof.

Let

L=F(ϕ(y):y∈X∖{a,b,c}).L=F\bigl(\phi(y):y\in X\setminus\{a,b,c\}\bigr).

By (7), every generator of LL is a cross-ratio of points of XX, so L⊆ℛF​(X)L\subseteq\mathscr{R}_{F}(X). Conversely, ϕ⁡(X)⊆ℙ1​(L)\phi(X)\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{1}(L) because ϕ⁡(a)=∞\phi(a)=\infty, ϕ⁡(b)=0\phi(b)=0, ϕ⁡(c)=1\phi(c)=1, and all remaining images belong to LL. For any four distinct points x1,x2,x3,x4∈Xx_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}\in X, projective invariance implies

χ⁡(x1,x2,x3,x4)=χ⁡(ϕ⁡(x1),ϕ⁡(x2),ϕ⁡(x3),ϕ⁡(x4))∈L.\chi(x_{1},x_{2};x_{3},x_{4})=\chi\bigl(\phi(x_{1}),\phi(x_{2});\phi(x_{3}),\phi(x_{4})\bigr)\in L.

Thus every generator of ℛF​(X)\mathscr{R}_{F}(X) lies in LL, proving the result. ∎

We now apply this field to the helper configuration Ω∖{αi}\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}. The use of the stabilizer of an aligned repair space to obtain a field-divisibility condition already appears in the lower-bound argument of Tamo, Ye, and Barg [18, proof of Theorem 5]. Here the relevant field is identified with the cross-ratio field of the helper points.

Proposition 1.

For every choice of BB and zz as in Lemma 2, the corresponding space AA is a ℛF​(Ω∖{αi})\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\})-linear subspace of KK. Consequently,

[ℛF(Ω∖{αi}):F]∣ℓs.\bigl[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}):F\bigr]\mid\frac{\ell}{s}.
Proof.

Let L=F(χ(x,z;bu,bv):x∈Ω∖(B∪{αi,z}),1≤u≠v≤s).L=F(\chi(x,z;b_{u},b_{v}):x\in\Omega\setminus(B\cup\{\alpha_{i},z\}),1\leq u\neq v\leq s). By Lemma 2, multiplication by each of these scalars maps AA onto itself. Consider

SA={λ∈K:λ​A⊆A}.S_{A}=\{\lambda\in K:\lambda A\subseteq A\}.

Since dimFA=ℓ/s>0\dim_{F}A=\ell/s>0, the space AA is nonzero. The set SAS_{A} contains FF and is closed under addition and multiplication. If 0≠λ∈SA0\neq\lambda\in S_{A}, then dimF(λ​A)=dimFA\dim_{F}(\lambda A)=\dim_{F}A, so λ​A=A\lambda A=A and λ−1​A=A\lambda^{-1}A=A. Hence SAS_{A} is a subfield of KK, and L⊆SAL\subseteq S_{A}.

We claim that

L=ℛF​(Ω∖{αi}).L=\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}).

The inclusion L⊆ℛF​(Ω∖{αi})L\subseteq\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}) is immediate. For the reverse inclusion, let ϕ=ϕb1,b2,z\phi=\phi_{b_{1},b_{2},z}. By Lemma 3, it is enough to show that ϕ⁡(y)∈L\phi(y)\in L for every y∈Ω∖{αi,b1,b2,z}y\in\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i},b_{1},b_{2},z\}. If y∉By\notin B, then

ϕ⁡(y)=χ⁡(y,z,b1,b2)∈L.\phi(y)=\chi(y,z;b_{1},b_{2})\in L.

Now let y=buy=b_{u} with u≥3u\geq 3. Since

|Ω∖(B∪{αi,z})|=k−2≥1,\bigl|\Omega\setminus(B\cup\{\alpha_{i},z\})\bigr|=k-2\geq 1,

choose ww in this set. Then

ϕ⁡(w)=χ⁡(w,z,b1,b2)∈L,cu:=χ⁡(w,z,b1,bu)∈L.\phi(w)=\chi(w,z;b_{1},b_{2})\in L,\qquad c_{u}:=\chi(w,z;b_{1},b_{u})\in L.

Using ϕ⁡(b1)=∞\phi(b_{1})=\infty, ϕ⁡(b2)=0\phi(b_{2})=0, and ϕ⁡(z)=1\phi(z)=1, projective invariance gives

cu=ϕ⁡(w)−ϕ⁡(bu)1−ϕ⁡(bu).c_{u}=\frac{\phi(w)-\phi(b_{u})}{1-\phi(b_{u})}.

If cu=1c_{u}=1, then ϕ⁡(w)=1=ϕ⁡(z)\phi(w)=1=\phi(z), contrary to the injectivity of ϕ\phi and w≠zw\neq z. Hence cu≠1c_{u}\neq 1, and

ϕ⁡(bu)=ϕ⁡(w)−cu1−cu∈L.\phi(b_{u})=\frac{\phi(w)-c_{u}}{1-c_{u}}\in L.

This proves the claim. Therefore AA is ℛF​(Ω∖{αi})\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\})-linear. Finally, dimFA=ℓ/s\dim_{F}A=\ell/s, so

ℓs=[ℛF(Ω∖{αi}):F]dimℛF​(Ω∖{αi})A,\frac{\ell}{s}=\bigl[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}):F\bigr]\dim_{\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\})}A,

which proves the divisibility. ∎

The failed coordinate imposes one further constraint. Fix B,z,AB,z,A as in Lemma 2. Put ρ1=1\rho_{1}=1 and, for 2≤u≤s2\leq u\leq s, define

ρu=hu​(αi)​h1​(z)h1​(αi)​hu​(z)=χ⁡(αi,z,bu,b1).\rho_{u}=\frac{h_{u}(\alpha_{i})h_{1}(z)}{h_{1}(\alpha_{i})h_{u}(z)}=\chi(\alpha_{i},z;b_{u},b_{1}). (8)
Proposition 2.

The elements ρ1,…,ρs\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{s} are linearly independent over ℛF​(Ω∖{αi})\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}). Consequently,

[ℛF(Ω):ℛF(Ω∖{αi})]≥s.\bigl[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega):\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\})\bigr]\geq s.
Proof.

Setting y=αiy=\alpha_{i} in (5) yields a surjective map

⨁u=1sUbu⟶K,(v1,…,vs)⟼∑u=1shu​(αi)​vu.\bigoplus_{u=1}^{s}U_{b_{u}}\longrightarrow K,\qquad(v_{1},\ldots,v_{s})\longmapsto\sum_{u=1}^{s}h_{u}(\alpha_{i})v_{u}.

Both spaces have FF-dimension ℓ\ell, so this map is an isomorphism. Equivalently,

K=⨁u=1shu​(αi)​Ubu.K=\bigoplus_{u=1}^{s}h_{u}(\alpha_{i})U_{b_{u}}. (9)

Set

A′=h1​(αi)h1​(z)​A.A^{\prime}=\frac{h_{1}(\alpha_{i})}{h_{1}(z)}A.

By Proposition 1, A′A^{\prime} is ℛF​(Ω∖{αi})\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\})-linear. Since A=hu​(z)​UbuA=h_{u}(z)U_{b_{u}}, (8) gives

ρu​A′=hu​(αi)​Ubu,1≤u≤s.\rho_{u}A^{\prime}=h_{u}(\alpha_{i})U_{b_{u}},\qquad 1\leq u\leq s.

Thus (9) becomes

K=⨁u=1sρu​A′.K=\bigoplus_{u=1}^{s}\rho_{u}A^{\prime}.

If

∑u=1scu​ρu=0,cu∈ℛF​(Ω∖{αi}),\sum_{u=1}^{s}c_{u}\rho_{u}=0,\qquad c_{u}\in\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}),

choose 0≠a∈A′0\neq a\in A^{\prime}. Multiplying the relation by aa and using cu​a∈A′c_{u}a\in A^{\prime}, the direct sum forces ρu​cu​a=0\rho_{u}c_{u}a=0 for every uu. Since ρu​a≠0\rho_{u}a\neq 0, we obtain cu=0c_{u}=0. Therefore the ρu\rho_{u} are linearly independent over the helper cross-ratio field. Since ρu∈ℛF​(Ω)\rho_{u}\in\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega), the relative degree is at least ss. ∎

We have proved that, whenever a coordinate has cut-set-optimal full-helper repair,

[ℛF(Ω∖{αi}):F]∣ℓs,[ℛF(Ω):ℛF(Ω∖{αi})]≥s.\bigl[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}):F\bigr]\mid\frac{\ell}{s},\qquad\bigl[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega):\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\})\bigr]\geq s.

These two degree constraints will be used repeatedly below.

III-B A General Lower Bound

To combine the degree constraints for different deleted coordinates, we first record a simple identity for cross-ratio fields.

Lemma 4.

Let A,B⊆ℙ1​(F¯)A,B\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{1}(\overline{F}) be finite sets with |A∩B|≥3|A\cap B|\geq 3. Then

ℛF​(A∪B)=ℛF​(A)​ℛF​(B),\mathscr{R}_{F}(A\cup B)=\mathscr{R}_{F}(A)\mathscr{R}_{F}(B),

where the right-hand side is the compositum inside F¯\overline{F}. In particular, if

X={α1,…,αm}⊆ℙ1​(F¯),m≥5,X=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{m}\}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{1}(\overline{F}),\qquad m\geq 5,

then, for distinct i,j∈[m]i,j\in[m],

ℛF​(X)=ℛF​(X∖{αi})​ℛF​(X∖{αj}).\mathscr{R}_{F}(X)=\mathscr{R}_{F}(X\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\})\mathscr{R}_{F}(X\setminus\{\alpha_{j}\}).
Proof.

The inclusion ℛF​(A)​ℛF​(B)⊆ℛF​(A∪B)\mathscr{R}_{F}(A)\mathscr{R}_{F}(B)\subseteq\mathscr{R}_{F}(A\cup B) follows from the definition. Choose distinct a,b,c∈A∩Ba,b,c\in A\cap B and let ϕ=ϕa,b,c\phi=\phi_{a,b,c}. By Lemma 3,

ℛF​(A)\displaystyle\mathscr{R}_{F}(A) =F(ϕ(y):y∈A∖{a,b,c}),\displaystyle=F\bigl(\phi(y):y\in A\setminus\{a,b,c\}\bigr),
ℛF​(B)\displaystyle\mathscr{R}_{F}(B) =F(ϕ(y):y∈B∖{a,b,c}),\displaystyle=F\bigl(\phi(y):y\in B\setminus\{a,b,c\}\bigr),
ℛF​(A∪B)\displaystyle\mathscr{R}_{F}(A\cup B) =F(ϕ(y):y∈(A∪B)∖{a,b,c}).\displaystyle=F\bigl(\phi(y):y\in(A\cup B)\setminus\{a,b,c\}\bigr).

The last field is generated by the first two, proving equality. The special case follows by taking A=X∖{αi}A=X\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\} and B=X∖{αj}B=X\setminus\{\alpha_{j}\}. ∎

For a configuration admitting cut-set-optimal full-helper repair of every coordinate, the degree lost when one evaluation point is deleted is at least ss. This leads to the following arithmetic quantity.

Definition 1.

For integers s≥2s\geq 2, define Gs​(0)=1G_{s}(0)=1. For an integer m≥1m\geq 1, minimize over integer tuples (g1,…,gm)(g_{1},\ldots,g_{m}):

Gs(m)=min{∏j=1mgj:gj≥s,gcd(gi,gj)=1 for i≠j}.G_{s}(m)=\min\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{m}g_{j}:g_{j}\geq s,\ \gcd(g_{i},g_{j})=1\text{ for }i\neq j\right\}.

Let pjp_{j} be the jj-th prime and write

pm#=∏j=1mpj,p0#=1.p_{m}^{\#}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}p_{j},\qquad p_{0}^{\#}=1.

In particular, G2​(m)=pm#G_{2}(m)=p_{m}^{\#}, and Gs​(m)≥pm#G_{s}(m)\geq p_{m}^{\#} for every s≥2s\geq 2.

Theorem 3.

Let F=𝔽qF=\mathbb{F}_{q} and K=𝔽qℓK=\mathbb{F}_{q^{\ell}}. Let k≥3k\geq 3, s=n−k≥2s=n-k\geq 2, and let Ω⊆K\Omega\subseteq K be an evaluation set of size nn. Suppose that RSK⁡(n,k,Ω)\operatorname{RS}_{K}(n,k,\Omega) admits cut-set-optimal FF-linear repair of every coordinate from all other n−1n-1 coordinates. Then

ℓ≥s​Gs​(n).\ell\geq sG_{s}(n).

More precisely, there exist pairwise coprime integers g1,…,gn≥sg_{1},\ldots,g_{n}\geq s such that

∏i=1ngi∣[ℛF(Ω):F]∣ℓs.\prod_{i=1}^{n}g_{i}\mid[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega):F]\mid\frac{\ell}{s}.
Proof.

Put

m=[ℛF(Ω):F],mi=[ℛF(Ω∖{αi}):F],gi=mmi.m=[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega):F],\qquad m_{i}=[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}):F],\qquad g_{i}=\frac{m}{m_{i}}.

By Propositions 1 and 2,

gi≥s,mi∣ℓs.g_{i}\geq s,\qquad m_{i}\mid\frac{\ell}{s}.

For distinct i,ji,j, Lemma 4 gives

ℛF​(Ω)=ℛF​(Ω∖{αi})​ℛF​(Ω∖{αj}).\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega)=\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\})\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{j}\}).

Finite subfields of F¯\overline{F} are determined by their degrees over FF, and the degree of their compositum is the least common multiple. Hence

m=lcm⁡(mi,mj).m=\operatorname{lcm}(m_{i},m_{j}).

Since mi,mj|ℓ/sm_{i},m_{j}\mid\ell/s, this also shows m|ℓ/sm\mid\ell/s. Moreover,

gi=mjgcd⁡(mi,mj),gj=migcd⁡(mi,mj),g_{i}=\frac{m_{j}}{\gcd(m_{i},m_{j})},\qquad g_{j}=\frac{m_{i}}{\gcd(m_{i},m_{j})},

so gcd⁡(gi,gj)=1\gcd(g_{i},g_{j})=1. Thus the gig_{i} are pairwise coprime. Each gig_{i} divides mm, so their product divides mm:

∏i=1ngi​∣m∣​ℓs.\prod_{i=1}^{n}g_{i}\mid m\mid\frac{\ell}{s}.

By the definition of Gs​(n)G_{s}(n), ∏igi≥Gs​(n)\prod_{i}g_{i}\geq G_{s}(n), and therefore ℓ≥s​Gs​(n)\ell\geq sG_{s}(n). ∎

A bound for arbitrary dd follows from the full-helper result by puncturing to one failed coordinate and its helpers.

Corollary 1.

Let k≥3k\geq 3 and s=d+1−k≥2s=d+1-k\geq 2. If an (n,k)(n,k) RS code admits cut-set-optimal FF-linear repair of every coordinate from every dd-helper set, then

ℓ≥s​Gs​(d+1).\ell\geq sG_{s}(d+1).
Proof.

Puncture the code to any d+1d+1 coordinates. For every coordinate in the punctured code, the other dd coordinates form an allowed helper set in the original code. Thus the punctured (d+1,k)(d+1,k) RS code admits cut-set-optimal full-helper repair of every coordinate. Applying Theorem 3 with n=d+1n=d+1 proves the claim. ∎

Remark 2.

Tamo, Ye, and Barg [18, Theorem 5] proved that every scalar linear MDS code admitting cut-set-optimal FF-linear repair of every coordinate from every dd-helper set satisfies

ℓ≥∏r=1k−1pr.\ell\geq\prod_{r=1}^{k-1}p_{r}.

Any d+1d+1 pairwise coprime integers at least s≥2s\geq 2 collectively contain at least d+1d+1 distinct prime divisors, and hence

Gs​(d+1)≥∏r=1d+1pr>∏r=1k−1pr.G_{s}(d+1)\geq\prod_{r=1}^{d+1}p_{r}>\prod_{r=1}^{k-1}p_{r}.

Thus, for RS codes, the general lower bound in Corollary 1 is stronger than that of [18, Theorem 5].

III-C An Improved Lower Bound for 2​d≥n+32d\geq n+3

The preceding bound uses only one set of d+1d+1 coordinates. We now use the constraints from all failed-coordinate/helper-set pairs. When 2​d≥n+32d\geq n+3, the resulting cross-ratio degrees admit an LCM representation, leading to the lower bound ℓ≥s​Δs​(n,d)\ell\geq s\Delta_{s}(n,d). We first record the degree constraints obtained from every punctured repair configuration.

Proposition 3.

Let k≥3k\geq 3 and s=d+1−k≥2s=d+1-k\geq 2. Suppose that RSK⁡(n,k,Ω)\operatorname{RS}_{K}(n,k,\Omega) admits cut-set-optimal FF-linear repair of every coordinate from every dd-helper set. Then, for every x∈Ωx\in\Omega and every H⊆Ω∖{x}H\subseteq\Omega\setminus\{x\} with |H|=d|H|=d,

[ℛF(H):F]∣ℓs,[ℛF(H∪{x}):ℛF(H)]≥s.[\mathscr{R}_{F}(H):F]\mid\frac{\ell}{s},\qquad[\mathscr{R}_{F}(H\cup\{x\}):\mathscr{R}_{F}(H)]\geq s.

Moreover,

[ℛF(Ω):F]∣ℓs.[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega):F]\mid\frac{\ell}{s}.
Proof.

Puncture to H∪{x}H\cup\{x\}. The resulting length-(d+1)(d+1) RS code admits cut-set-optimal full-helper repair of each of its coordinates. Applying Propositions 1 and 2 with target xx yields

[ℛF(H):F]∣ℓs,[ℛF(H∪{x}):ℛF(H)]≥s.[\mathscr{R}_{F}(H):F]\mid\frac{\ell}{s},\qquad[\mathscr{R}_{F}(H\cup\{x\}):\mathscr{R}_{F}(H)]\geq s.

It remains to prove the global divisibility. Since d≥4d\geq 4, every four-point subset of Ω\Omega lies in some dd-subset HH. Thus ℛF​(Ω)\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega) is the compositum of the fields ℛF​(H)\mathscr{R}_{F}(H) over all dd-subsets. By the finite-field compositum formula and the first part,

[ℛF(Ω):F]=lcmH⊆Ω|H|=d[ℛF(H):F]∣ℓs.[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega):F]=\operatorname{lcm}_{\begin{subarray}{c}H\subseteq\Omega\\ |H|=d\end{subarray}}[\mathscr{R}_{F}(H):F]\mid\frac{\ell}{s}.

∎

We next define the arithmetic quantity that will also appear in the construction.

Definition 2.

Let s,N,ts,N,t be integers with s≥2s\geq 2 and 1≤t<N1\leq t<N. A tuple of positive integers (a1,…,aN)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}) is feasible for (N,t,s)(N,t,s) if

lcm(aj:j∈J∪{i})lcm(aj:j∈J)≥s\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(a_{j}:j\in J\cup\{i\})}{\operatorname{lcm}(a_{j}:j\in J)}\geq s

for every i∈[N]i\in[N] and every tt-subset J⊆[N]∖{i}J\subseteq[N]\setminus\{i\}. Define Δs​(N,t)\Delta_{s}(N,t) as the minimum of lcm⁡(a1,…,aN)\operatorname{lcm}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}) over all feasible tuples.

Thus Δs​(N,t)\Delta_{s}(N,t) is the minimum lcm compatible with all the above relative-degree inequalities. Any NN pairwise coprime integers at least ss form a feasible tuple, so

Δs​(N,t)≤Gs​(N).\Delta_{s}(N,t)\leq G_{s}(N). (10)

The following elementary lemma converts identities of the form mS∩T=lcm⁡(mS,mT)m_{S\cap T}=\operatorname{lcm}(m_{S},m_{T}) into a representation by coordinate labels.

Lemma 5.

Let 0≤r<n0\leq r<n, and let mTm_{T} be a positive integer for every T⊆[n]T\subseteq[n] with |T|≤r|T|\leq r. The following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    for every such S,TS,T,

    mS∩T=lcm⁡(mS,mT);m_{S\cap T}=\operatorname{lcm}(m_{S},m_{T});
  2. 2.

    there exist positive integers b1,…,bnb_{1},\ldots,b_{n} such that

    mT=lcm(bi:i∉T)m_{T}=\operatorname{lcm}(b_{i}:i\notin T)

    for every |T|≤r|T|\leq r.

One possible choice is

bi=gcd(mR:|R|≤r,i∉R).b_{i}=\gcd(m_{R}:|R|\leq r,\ i\notin R).
Proof.

Assume the first condition. If R⊆VR\subseteq V, then

mR=lcm⁡(mR,mV),m_{R}=\operatorname{lcm}(m_{R},m_{V}),

so mV|mRm_{V}\mid m_{R}. Fix a prime pp. For a positive integer aa, vp​(a)v_{p}(a) denotes the exponent of pp in the prime factorization of aa. Write

eT=vp​(mT),λi=min|R|≤ri∉R⁡eR.e_{T}=v_{p}(m_{T}),\qquad\lambda_{i}=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}|R|\leq r\\ i\notin R\end{subarray}}e_{R}.

For i∉Ti\notin T, we have λi≤eT\lambda_{i}\leq e_{T}. We claim that equality holds for at least one such ii. Otherwise, for each i∉Ti\notin T choose RiR_{i} with i∉Rii\notin R_{i} and eRi=λi<eTe_{R_{i}}=\lambda_{i}<e_{T}, and put

R=⋂i∉TRi.R=\mathop{\bigcap}\limits_{i\notin T}R_{i}.

For every i∉Ti\notin T, the point ii is missing from RiR_{i}, hence from RR; therefore R⊆TR\subseteq T. Repeated application of the first condition yields

eR=maxi∉T⁡eRi<eT.e_{R}=\max_{i\notin T}e_{R_{i}}<e_{T}.

But R⊆TR\subseteq T implies mT|mRm_{T}\mid m_{R}, hence eT≤eRe_{T}\leq e_{R}, a contradiction. Thus

eT=maxi∉T⁡λi.e_{T}=\max_{i\notin T}\lambda_{i}.

Since vp​(bi)=λiv_{p}(b_{i})=\lambda_{i}, this is exactly the pp-adic valuation of lcm(bi:i∉T)\operatorname{lcm}(b_{i}:i\notin T). As this holds for every prime,

mT=lcm(bi:i∉T).m_{T}=\operatorname{lcm}(b_{i}:i\notin T).

Conversely, if such a representation holds, then

[n]∖(S∩T)=([n]∖S)∪([n]∖T),[n]\setminus(S\cap T)=([n]\setminus S)\cup([n]\setminus T),

and the desired lcm identity follows immediately. ∎

Suppose now that 2​d≥n+32d\geq n+3. If S,T⊆[n]S,T\subseteq[n] have |S|,|T|≤n−d|S|,|T|\leq n-d, then at least three evaluation points remain after deleting S∪TS\cup T. This allows the preceding lcm representation to be applied simultaneously to all relevant cross-ratio fields.

Theorem 4.

Let 3≤k<d≤n−13\leq k<d\leq n-1, put s=d+1−ks=d+1-k, and suppose that RSK⁡(n,k,Ω)\operatorname{RS}_{K}(n,k,\Omega) admits cut-set-optimal FF-linear repair of every coordinate from every dd-helper set. If

2​d≥n+3,2d\geq n+3,

then there exist positive integers b1,…,bnb_{1},\ldots,b_{n} such that, for any T⊆[n]T\subseteq[n] with |T|≤n−d|T|\leq n-d,

[ℛF({αj:j∉T}):F]=lcm(bj:j∉T)[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\{\alpha_{j}:j\notin T\}):F]=\operatorname{lcm}(b_{j}:j\notin T) (11)

and

lcm(b1,…,bn)=[ℛF(Ω):F]∣ℓs.\operatorname{lcm}(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n})=[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega):F]\mid\frac{\ell}{s}. (12)

Moreover, (b1,…,bn)(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}) is feasible for (n,d,s)(n,d,s). Consequently,

ℓ≥s​Δs​(n,d),\ell\geq s\Delta_{s}(n,d),

and hence

ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≥s​Δs​(n,d).\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\geq s\Delta_{s}(n,d).
Proof.

Put r=n−dr=n-d. For T⊆[n]T\subseteq[n] with |T|≤r|T|\leq r, put

XT={αj:j∉T},mT=[ℛF(XT):F].X_{T}=\{\alpha_{j}:j\notin T\},\qquad m_{T}=[\mathscr{R}_{F}(X_{T}):F].

For two such sets S,TS,T,

|XS∩XT|=n−|S∪T|≥n−2​r=2​d−n≥3.|X_{S}\cap X_{T}|=n-|S\cup T|\geq n-2r=2d-n\geq 3.

Moreover, XS∪XT=XS∩TX_{S}\cup X_{T}=X_{S\cap T}. Hence Lemma 4 gives

ℛF​(XS∩T)=ℛF​(XS)​ℛF​(XT),\mathscr{R}_{F}(X_{S\cap T})=\mathscr{R}_{F}(X_{S})\mathscr{R}_{F}(X_{T}),

and therefore, since the fields are finite,

mS∩T=lcm⁡(mS,mT).m_{S\cap T}=\operatorname{lcm}(m_{S},m_{T}).

By Lemma 5, there are positive integers b1,…,bnb_{1},\ldots,b_{n} satisfying (11). Taking T=∅T=\varnothing yields the first equality in (12), while Proposition 3 shows that [ℛF(Ω):F][\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega):F] divides ℓ/s\ell/s.

It remains to verify feasibility. Let H⊆[n]H\subseteq[n] have size dd and let i∉Hi\notin H. Put T=[n]∖HT=[n]\setminus H, so |T|=r|T|=r and i∈Ti\in T. Applying (11) to TT and T∖{i}T\setminus\{i\} gives

lcm⁡(bi,{bh:h∈H})lcm(bh:h∈H)=[ℛF({αh:h∈H}∪{αi}):ℛF({αh:h∈H})].\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(b_{i},\{b_{h}:h\in H\})}{\operatorname{lcm}(b_{h}:h\in H)}=[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\{\alpha_{h}:h\in H\}\cup\{\alpha_{i}\}):\mathscr{R}_{F}(\{\alpha_{h}:h\in H\})].

The right-hand side is at least ss by Proposition 3. Thus the tuple is feasible, and

Δs(n,d)≤lcm(b1,…,bn)=[ℛF(Ω):F]≤ℓs,\Delta_{s}(n,d)\leq\operatorname{lcm}(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n})=[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega):F]\leq\frac{\ell}{s},

where the divisibility underlying the last inequality was established in (12). ∎

III-D A Stronger Lower Bound for d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1)

We now establish the bound ℓ≥s​Gs​(n)\ell\geq sG_{s}(n) under d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1), extending beyond the range 2​d≥n+32d\geq n+3. When 2​d<n+32d<n+3, two dd-subsets may intersect in fewer than three points, so the preceding LCM representation is no longer guaranteed by the overlap argument. We therefore work directly with the degrees of the cross-ratio fields and track how they change when individual evaluation points are deleted.

For every Y⊆ΩY\subseteq\Omega with |Y|≥3|Y|\geq 3, write

m(Y)=[ℛF(Y):F],M=m(Ω).m(Y)=[\mathscr{R}_{F}(Y):F],\qquad M=m(\Omega).

For i∈[n]i\in[n], put

mi=m⁡(Ω∖{αi}),gi=Mmi.m_{i}=m(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}),\qquad g_{i}=\frac{M}{m_{i}}.

Thus gig_{i} measures the part of the total degree that disappears when αi\alpha_{i} is deleted. We call coordinate ii nondeficient if gi≥sg_{i}\geq s, and deficient if gi<sg_{i}<s. Let

ℬ={i:gi<s},b=|ℬ|.\mathcal{B}=\{i:g_{i}<s\},\qquad b=|\mathcal{B}|.

The nondeficient coordinates already contribute individual factors of size at least ss. For a deficient coordinate, the additional factor required by the repair constraint must come from prime powers shared with other coordinates. The next lemma makes this decomposition precise.

Lemma 6.

The integers g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n} are pairwise coprime. Put

M0:=M∏i=1ngi.M_{0}:=\frac{M}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}g_{i}}.

Then M0M_{0} is a positive integer satisfying

M0=gcd⁡(m1,…,mn),⋂i=1nℛF​(Ω∖{αi})=𝔽qM0.M_{0}=\gcd(m_{1},\ldots,m_{n}),\qquad\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\})=\mathbb{F}_{q^{M_{0}}}.

Moreover,

M≥M0​Gs​(n−b).M\geq M_{0}G_{s}(n-b). (13)
Proof.

For distinct i,ji,j, the sets Ω∖{αi}\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\} and Ω∖{αj}\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{j}\} intersect in at least three points. By Lemma 4,

M=lcm⁡(mi,mj).M=\operatorname{lcm}(m_{i},m_{j}).

Fix a prime p|Mp\mid M, and write E=vp​(M)E=v_{p}(M) and ei=vp​(mi)e_{i}=v_{p}(m_{i}). Thus E=max⁡{ei,ej}E=\max\{e_{i},e_{j}\} for every i≠ji\neq j, so at most one eie_{i} is smaller than EE. As vp​(gi)=E−eiv_{p}(g_{i})=E-e_{i}, at most one gig_{i} is divisible by pp. Hence the gig_{i} are pairwise coprime and ∏igi|M\prod_{i}g_{i}\mid M. Furthermore,

vp​(M0)\displaystyle v_{p}(M_{0}) =E−∑i=1n(E−ei)=min1≤i≤n⁡ei=vp​(gcd⁡(m1,…,mn)).\displaystyle=E-\sum_{i=1}^{n}(E-e_{i})=\min_{1\leq i\leq n}e_{i}=v_{p}(\gcd(m_{1},\ldots,m_{n})).

The same equality is immediate for p∤Mp\nmid M, proving the gcd identity. The finite-field intersection formula now yields

⋂i=1nℛF​(Ω∖{αi})=⋂i=1n𝔽qmi=𝔽qgcd⁡(m1,…,mn)=𝔽qM0.\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\})=\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{F}_{q^{m_{i}}}=\mathbb{F}_{q^{\gcd(m_{1},\ldots,m_{n})}}=\mathbb{F}_{q^{M_{0}}}.

Finally, the n−bn-b nondeficient gig_{i} are pairwise coprime and at least ss, whence

M=M0​∏i=1ngi≥M0​Gs​(n−b).M=M_{0}\prod_{i=1}^{n}g_{i}\geq M_{0}G_{s}(n-b).

∎

Although the gig_{i} are pairwise coprime, they need not be coprime to M0M_{0}. The factor M0M_{0} is common to the cross-ratio fields obtained by deleting any one point. The next lemma tracks how much of this common degree is generated by an arbitrary subset.

Lemma 7.

For Y⊆ΩY\subseteq\Omega with |Y|≥3|Y|\geq 3, define

D⁡(Y)=gcd⁡(m⁡(Y),M0).D(Y)=\gcd(m(Y),M_{0}).

Then

D(Y)=[ℛF(Y)∩𝔽qM0:F].D(Y)=[\mathscr{R}_{F}(Y)\cap\mathbb{F}_{q^{M_{0}}}:F].

For every Y⊆ΩY\subseteq\Omega with |Y|≥4|Y|\geq 4,

m⁡(Y)=D⁡(Y)​∏αi∈Ygi.m(Y)=D(Y)\prod_{\alpha_{i}\in Y}g_{i}. (14)

Moreover, D⁡(A)|D⁡(B)D(A)\mid D(B) whenever A⊆BA\subseteq B and |A|≥3|A|\geq 3; if |A∩B|≥3|A\cap B|\geq 3, then

D⁡(A∪B)=lcm⁡(D⁡(A),D⁡(B)).D(A\cup B)=\operatorname{lcm}(D(A),D(B)).

In particular, for every ii and every dd-subset H⊆Ω∖{αi}H\subseteq\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\},

m⁡(H∪{αi})m⁡(H)=gi​D⁡(H∪{αi})D⁡(H).\frac{m(H\cup\{\alpha_{i}\})}{m(H)}=g_{i}\frac{D(H\cup\{\alpha_{i}\})}{D(H)}. (15)
Proof.

The finite-field intersection formula gives

ℛF​(Y)∩𝔽qM0=𝔽qgcd⁡(m⁡(Y),M0)=𝔽qD⁡(Y),\mathscr{R}_{F}(Y)\cap\mathbb{F}_{q^{M_{0}}}=\mathbb{F}_{q^{\gcd(m(Y),M_{0})}}=\mathbb{F}_{q^{D(Y)}},

which proves the claimed field interpretation.

To prove (14), fix a prime p|Mp\mid M and write

E=vp​(M),ei=vp​(mi),Cp=vp​(M0)=mini⁡ei.E=v_{p}(M),\qquad e_{i}=v_{p}(m_{i}),\qquad C_{p}=v_{p}(M_{0})=\min_{i}e_{i}.

By the proof of Lemma 6, at most one eie_{i} is smaller than EE, and vp​(gi)=E−eiv_{p}(g_{i})=E-e_{i}. Also,

vp​(D⁡(Y))=min⁡{vp​(m⁡(Y)),Cp}.v_{p}(D(Y))=\min\{v_{p}(m(Y)),C_{p}\}.

If every ei=Ee_{i}=E, then Cp=EC_{p}=E and pp divides none of the gig_{i}; both sides of (14) have pp-adic exponent vp​(m​(Y))v_{p}(m(Y)). Otherwise, let jj be the unique index with ej=Cp<Ee_{j}=C_{p}<E. Then vp​(gj)=E−Cpv_{p}(g_{j})=E-C_{p}, while vp​(gi)=0v_{p}(g_{i})=0 for i≠ji\neq j. If αj∉Y\alpha_{j}\notin Y, then Y⊆Ω∖{αj}Y\subseteq\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{j}\}, so vp​(m⁡(Y))≤Cpv_{p}(m(Y))\leq C_{p} and vp​(D⁡(Y))=vp​(m⁡(Y))v_{p}(D(Y))=v_{p}(m(Y)). If αj∈Y\alpha_{j}\in Y and |Y|≥4|Y|\geq 4, then

Y∪(Ω∖{αj})=Ω,|Y∩(Ω∖{αj})|≥3.Y\cup(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{j}\})=\Omega,\qquad|Y\cap(\Omega\setminus\{\alpha_{j}\})|\geq 3.

Therefore Lemma 4 yields

M=lcm⁡(m⁡(Y),mj),M=\operatorname{lcm}(m(Y),m_{j}),

so vp​(m​(Y))=Ev_{p}(m(Y))=E because Cp<EC_{p}<E. The exponent on the right of (14) is then Cp+(E−Cp)=EC_{p}+(E-C_{p})=E. The equality is trivial for p∤Mp\nmid M, proving (14).

If A⊆BA\subseteq B, then m⁡(A)|m⁡(B)m(A)\mid m(B), and hence D⁡(A)|D⁡(B)D(A)\mid D(B). If |A∩B|≥3|A\cap B|\geq 3, Lemma 4 gives m⁡(A∪B)=lcm⁡(m⁡(A),m⁡(B))m(A\cup B)=\operatorname{lcm}(m(A),m(B)). For any prime pp, writing c=vp​(M0)c=v_{p}(M_{0}), we have

vp​(D​(A∪B))\displaystyle v_{p}(D(A\cup B)) =min⁡{max⁡(vp​(m⁡(A)),vp​(m⁡(B))),c}\displaystyle=\min\{\max(v_{p}(m(A)),v_{p}(m(B))),c\}
=max⁡{min⁡(vp​(m⁡(A)),c),min⁡(vp​(m⁡(B)),c)}\displaystyle=\max\{\min(v_{p}(m(A)),c),\min(v_{p}(m(B)),c)\}
=vp​(lcm⁡(D⁡(A),D⁡(B))).\displaystyle=v_{p}(\operatorname{lcm}(D(A),D(B))).

This proves the lcm identity. Finally, d≥4d\geq 4 ensures that both HH and H∪{αi}H\cup\{\alpha_{i}\} satisfy (14). Dividing the two factorizations yields (15). ∎

For a deficient coordinate ii, the factor gig_{i} in (15) is strictly smaller than ss. On the other hand, Proposition 3 requires

m⁡(H∪{αi})m⁡(H)≥s\frac{m(H\cup\{\alpha_{i}\})}{m(H)}\geq s

for every dd-helper set HH. By (15), this forces D⁡(H∪{αi})/D⁡(H)≥s/gi>1D(H\cup\{\alpha_{i}\})/D(H)\geq s/g_{i}>1: the missing factor must come from the shared part. The next lemma quantifies how many distinct prime divisors of M0M_{0} are forced in this way. For a positive integer NN, let ω⁡(N)\omega(N) denote the number of distinct prime divisors of NN.

Lemma 8.

Use the notation above. Let W⊆ΩW\subseteq\Omega satisfy 4≤w:=|W|≤d+14\leq w:=|W|\leq d+1. For every deficient coordinate i∈ℬi\in\mathcal{B} with αi∈W\alpha_{i}\in W, put

Wi=W∖{αi},qi​(W)=D⁡(W)D⁡(Wi).W_{i}=W\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\},\qquad q_{i}(W)=\frac{D(W)}{D(W_{i})}.

Then qi​(W)q_{i}(W) is a positive integer dividing M0M_{0}, and

ω⁡(qi​(W))≥d−w+2.\omega(q_{i}(W))\geq d-w+2. (16)

If i≠ji\neq j are deficient coordinates with αi,αj∈W\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}\in W and w≥5w\geq 5, then

gcd⁡(qi​(W),qj​(W))=1.\gcd(q_{i}(W),q_{j}(W))=1.

Consequently, if b≥1b\geq 1, then

ω⁡(M0)≥d−2,\omega(M_{0})\geq d-2, (17)

and, for every 1≤u≤min⁡{b,d+1}1\leq u\leq\min\{b,d+1\},

ω⁡(M0)≥u⁡(d+2−max⁡{5,u}).\omega(M_{0})\geq u\bigl(d+2-\max\{5,u\}\bigr). (18)
Proof.

Since Wi⊆WW_{i}\subseteq W, Lemma 7 gives D⁡(Wi)|D⁡(W)D(W_{i})\mid D(W), so qi​(W)q_{i}(W) is an integer. Moreover D⁡(W)|M0D(W)\mid M_{0}, and hence every prime divisor of qi​(W)q_{i}(W) divides M0M_{0}.

IV Construction and Minimum Subpacketization

In this section, we construct RS codes with subpacketization s​Δs​(n,d)s\Delta_{s}(n,d) for every admissible choice of parameters. Combining this construction with the lower bound from Section III determines the minimum subpacketization when d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1). We then derive an exact threshold for a closed-form expression for Gs​(m)G_{s}(m) and a finite formula valid for all mm.

IV-A Construction from Feasible Degree Tuples

The feasibility condition defining Δs​(n,d)\Delta_{s}(n,d) is exactly the relative-degree condition needed to apply Theorem 2.

Indeed, for a failed coordinate ii and a helper set HH, if [F(αj):F]=aj[F(\alpha_{j}):F]=a_{j} and FH=F(αh:h∈H)F_{H}=F(\alpha_{h}:h\in H), then the compositum rule for finite fields gives

[FH(αi):FH]=lcm⁡(ai,{ah:h∈H})lcm(ah:h∈H).[F_{H}(\alpha_{i}):F_{H}]=\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(a_{i},\{a_{h}:h\in H\})}{\operatorname{lcm}(a_{h}:h\in H)}.

Thus feasibility guarantees that this relative degree is at least ss. Consequently, Theorem 2 provides the required repair subspace for every such pair (i,H)(i,H). A dual check polynomial vanishing at the nonhelpers then restricts the parity-check equations to H∪{i}H\cup\{i\}.

symbols over FF. The total repair bandwidth is therefore d​M=d​ℓ/sdM=d\ell/s, exactly the cut-set bound. Since (i,H)(i,H) was arbitrary, the code admits optimal FF-linear repair in every required repair configuration. ∎

Remark 3.

The values Λi,H​(αh)\Lambda_{i,H}(\alpha_{h}) need not lie in FHF_{H}, because only the factors αhu\alpha_{h}^{u} are moved through the trace. Moreover, the repair subspace may depend on (i,H)(i,H): the model requires an optimal scheme for every repair scenario, not a common repair space across all scenarios.

IV-B Exact Minimum Subpacketization for d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1)

The construction above and the lower bound from Theorem 5 together yield the following exact formula.

Theorem 7.

Let 3≤k<d≤n−13\leq k<d\leq n-1, put s=d+1−ks=d+1-k, and let qq be any prime power. If

d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1),d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1),

then

ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=s​Δs​(n,d)=s​Gs​(n).\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=s\Delta_{s}(n,d)=sG_{s}(n).
Proof.

By Theorems 5 and 6 and (10),

s​Gs​(n)≤ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≤s​Δs​(n,d)≤s​Gs​(n).sG_{s}(n)\leq\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\leq s\Delta_{s}(n,d)\leq sG_{s}(n).

Hence equality holds throughout. ∎

In their survey, Ramkumar et al. [23, Open Problem 20] asked for the minimum subpacketization of an RS code that attains the cut-set bound in the full-helper case d=n−1d=n-1. For exact linear repair in the range 3≤k<n−13\leq k<n-1, the preceding theorem resolves the corresponding case of Open Problem 20. The resulting formula is recorded below.

Corollary 2.

Let d=n−1d=n-1 and s=n−ks=n-k, where 3≤k<n−13\leq k<n-1. Then, for every prime power qq,

ℓmin​(n,k,n−1,q)=s​Δs​(n,n−1)=s​Gs​(n).\ell_{\min}(n,k,n-1;q)=s\Delta_{s}(n,n-1)=sG_{s}(n).
Proof.

Here n≥5n\geq 5, and

(n−1)​(n+1)−4​(n+1)=(n+1)​(n−5)≥0.(n-1)(n+1)-4(n+1)=(n+1)(n-5)\geq 0.

Hence the quadratic condition holds with d=n−1d=n-1, and Theorem 7 applies. ∎

Combining the threshold with Theorem 7 yields the following closed form whenever d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1).

Corollary 3.

Let qq be a prime power, 3≤k<d≤n−13\leq k<d\leq n-1, and s=d+1−ks=d+1-k. Assume d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1). Then

For every fixed integer s≥2s\geq 2, as m→∞m\to\infty,

log⁡Gs​(m)=(1+o⁡(1))​m​log⁡m.\log G_{s}(m)=(1+o(1))m\log m.
Proof.

For m≥σsm\geq\sigma_{s}, use Theorem 8 and log⁡pm#∼m​log⁡m\log p_{m}^{\#}\sim m\log m from the prime number theorem [25]. ∎

The preceding theorem provides a closed form for Gs​(m)G_{s}(m) when m≥σsm\geq\sigma_{s}. We now give a finite formula valid also below this threshold. For each nonempty set BB of primes below ss, the integer μs​(B)\mu_{s}(B) can be computed by

μs(B)=min{∏p∈Bpep:1≤ep≤⌈logps⌉,∏p∈Bpep≥s},\mu_{s}(B)=\min\left\{\prod_{p\in B}p^{e_{p}}:1\leq e_{p}\leq\lceil\log_{p}s\rceil,\quad\prod_{p\in B}p^{e_{p}}\geq s\right\},

where the exponents are integers. Indeed, an exponent exceeding ⌈logp⁡s⌉\lceil\log_{p}s\rceil can be reduced to this value without changing the set of prime divisors or making the product less than ss.

Theorem 9.

Let s≥2s\geq 2 and m≥0m\geq 0. For each integer 0≤r≤min⁡{m,cs}0\leq r\leq\min\{m,c_{s}\}, let B1,…,BrB_{1},\ldots,B_{r} range over pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets of {p1,…,pcs}\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{c_{s}}\}. Then

Gs​(m)=min0≤r≤min⁡{m,cs}B1,…,Br⁡(∏j=1rμs​(Bj))​pm+cs−r#pcs#.G_{s}(m)=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq r\leq\min\{m,c_{s}\}\\ B_{1},\ldots,B_{r}\end{subarray}}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{r}\mu_{s}(B_{j})\right)\frac{p_{m+c_{s}-r}^{\#}}{p_{c_{s}}^{\#}}. (27)

For r=0r=0, the tuple is empty and its product is 11. If m≥σsm\geq\sigma_{s}, a minimizing choice is r=csr=c_{s} and Bj={pj}B_{j}=\{p_{j}\} for 1≤j≤cs1\leq j\leq c_{s}.

Proof.

Choose pairwise coprime integers x1,…,xm≥sx_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\geq s whose product is Gs​(m)G_{s}(m). As in the proof of Theorem 8, any xjx_{j} with a prime divisor at least ss must equal that prime: otherwise, replacing xjx_{j} by the prime would decrease the product and preserve admissibility. Likewise, if all prime divisors of xjx_{j} are below ss, minimality forces xj=μs​(B)x_{j}=\mu_{s}(B), where BB is its set of prime divisors.

After reordering, suppose the latter type occurs rr times, with prime-divisor sets B1,…,BrB_{1},\ldots,B_{r}. These sets are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, and contained in {p1,…,pcs}\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{c_{s}}\}; in particular, 0≤r≤min⁡{m,cs}0\leq r\leq\min\{m,c_{s}\}. The remaining m−rm-r factors are distinct primes at least ss. Their product is at least the product of the first m−rm-r primes at least ss, namely

∏j=cs+1cs+m−rpj=pm+cs−r#pcs#.\prod_{j=c_{s}+1}^{c_{s}+m-r}p_{j}=\frac{p_{m+c_{s}-r}^{\#}}{p_{c_{s}}^{\#}}.

Conversely, fix any rr and B1,…,BrB_{1},\ldots,B_{r} allowed in the theorem. The mm integers

μs​(B1),…,μs​(Br),pcs+1,…,pcs+m−r\mu_{s}(B_{1}),\ldots,\mu_{s}(B_{r}),\quad p_{c_{s}+1},\ldots,p_{c_{s}+m-r}

are all at least ss and are pairwise coprime: the BjB_{j} are disjoint and contain only primes below ss, while the remaining factors are distinct primes at least ss. Their product equals the corresponding expression in (27), proving the reverse inequality.

Finally, let m≥σsm\geq\sigma_{s} and choose r=csr=c_{s} and Bj={pj}B_{j}=\{p_{j}\}. Since μs​({pj})=apj\mu_{s}(\{p_{j}\})=a_{p_{j}}, (24) gives

V Asymptotics for Fixed kk and dd

Fix a prime power qq and integers 3≤k<d3\leq k<d, put s=d+1−ks=d+1-k, and let n→∞n\to\infty with kk and dd fixed. We determine the order of log⁡ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)\log\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q). The lower bound comes from counting distinct subset least common multiples, while the upper bound uses cover-free families. All logarithms in this section are natural.

Let τ⁡(M)\tau(M) denote the number of positive divisors of a positive integer MM. For x≥1x\geq 1, define

𝔇(x)=min{M∈ℤ:M≥1,τ(M)≥x}.\mathfrak{D}(x)=\min\{M\in\mathbb{Z}:M\geq 1,\ \tau(M)\geq x\}. (28)
Lemma 11.

Let (a1,…,aN)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}) be a feasible (N,t,s)(N,t,s)-tuple, where s≥2s\geq 2 and 1≤t<N1\leq t<N, and put M=lcm⁡(a1,…,aN)M=\operatorname{lcm}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}). Then

τ⁡(M)≥∑r=0t(Nr).\tau(M)\geq\sum_{r=0}^{t}\binom{N}{r}.

Consequently,

Δs​(N,t)≥𝔇⁡(∑r=0t(Nr)).\Delta_{s}(N,t)\geq\mathfrak{D}\!\left(\sum_{r=0}^{t}\binom{N}{r}\right).
Proof.

For A⊆[N]A\subseteq[N], write LA=lcm(ai:i∈A)L_{A}=\operatorname{lcm}(a_{i}:i\in A), with L∅=1L_{\varnothing}=1. We claim that for |A|,|B|≤t|A|,|B|\leq t,

LA|LB⟹A⊆B.L_{A}\mid L_{B}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A\subseteq B.

Otherwise, take i∈A∖Bi\in A\setminus B. Since |B|≤t<N|B|\leq t<N, we may extend BB to a tt-subset J⊆[N]∖{i}J\subseteq[N]\setminus\{i\}. Then ai|LA​∣LB∣​LJa_{i}\mid L_{A}\mid L_{B}\mid L_{J}, and hence

LJ∪{i}LJ=1<s,\frac{L_{J\cup\{i\}}}{L_{J}}=1<s,

contrary to feasibility. In particular, LA=LBL_{A}=L_{B} implies A=BA=B whenever |A|,|B|≤t|A|,|B|\leq t. These ∑r=0t(Nr)\sum_{r=0}^{t}\binom{N}{r} distinct values are all divisors of MM, which proves the first assertion. The second follows from (28) and the definition of Δs​(N,t)\Delta_{s}(N,t). ∎

To use this counting bound, we need the asymptotic growth of 𝔇⁡(x)\mathfrak{D}(x). The following lemma is a direct consequence of Wigert’s theorem on the maximal order of the divisor function.

Lemma 12.

As x→∞x\to\infty,

log⁡𝔇⁡(x)=(1log⁡2+o⁡(1))​log⁡x​log⁡log⁡x.\log\mathfrak{D}(x)=\left(\frac{1}{\log 2}+o(1)\right)\log x\log\log x. (29)
Proof.

For Y≥1Y\geq 1, let

H⁡(Y)=maxM∈ℤ1≤M≤Y⁡log⁡τ⁡(M).H(Y)=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\in\mathbb{Z}\\ 1\leq M\leq Y\end{subarray}}\log\tau(M).

Wigert’s theorem [26], in the formulation given in [27], states that

H⁡(Y)=(log⁡2+o⁡(1))​log⁡Ylog⁡log⁡Y(Y→∞).H(Y)=(\log 2+o(1))\frac{\log Y}{\log\log Y}\qquad(Y\to\infty).

For x≥1x\geq 1 and Y≥1Y\geq 1, the definitions yield the equivalence

H(Y)≥logx⟺𝔇(x)≤Y.H(Y)\geq\log x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathfrak{D}(x)\leq Y.

Fix ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) and, for xx sufficiently large, set

Y±=exp⁡(1±εlog⁡2​log⁡x​log⁡log⁡x).Y_{\pm}=\exp\!\left(\frac{1\pm\varepsilon}{\log 2}\log x\log\log x\right).

Since

log⁡log⁡Y±=log⁡log⁡x+log⁡log⁡log⁡x+Oε​(1)=(1+o⁡(1))​log​log⁡x,\log\log Y_{\pm}=\log\log x+\log\log\log x+O_{\varepsilon}(1)=(1+o(1))\log\log x,

Wigert’s theorem yields

H⁡(Y±)=(1±ε+o⁡(1))​log⁡x.H(Y_{\pm})=(1\pm\varepsilon+o(1))\log x.

Thus, for all sufficiently large xx,

H⁡(Y−)<log⁡x<H⁡(Y+),H(Y_{-})<\log x<H(Y_{+}),

and the preceding equivalence gives

Y−<𝔇⁡(x)≤Y+.Y_{-}<\mathfrak{D}(x)\leq Y_{+}.

Taking logarithms and then letting ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 proves (29). ∎

For the upper bound, recall that a family 𝒜={A1,…,AN}⊆2[m]\mathcal{A}=\{A_{1},\ldots,A_{N}\}\subseteq 2^{[m]} is tt-cover-free if

Ai⊈⋃j∈JAjA_{i}\not\subseteq\bigcup_{j\in J}A_{j}

for every i∈[N]i\in[N] and every tt-subset J⊆[N]∖{i}J\subseteq[N]\setminus\{i\}. Let mcff​(N,t)m_{\mathrm{cff}}(N,t) be the minimum possible size mm of the ground set.

Lemma 13.

For integers s≥2s\geq 2 and 1≤t<N1\leq t<N,

Δs​(N,t)≤Gs​(mcff​(N,t)).\Delta_{s}(N,t)\leq G_{s}(m_{\mathrm{cff}}(N,t)). (30)

Consequently, for every prime power qq and 3≤k<d≤n−13\leq k<d\leq n-1, with s=d+1−ks=d+1-k,

ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≤s​Gs​(mcff​(n,d)).\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\leq sG_{s}(m_{\mathrm{cff}}(n,d)). (31)
Proof.

Choose a tt-cover-free family 𝒜={A1,…,AN}\mathcal{A}=\{A_{1},\ldots,A_{N}\} on [m][m] and pairwise coprime integers g1,…,gm≥sg_{1},\ldots,g_{m}\geq s such that ∏r=1mgr=Gs​(m)\prod_{r=1}^{m}g_{r}=G_{s}(m). Set

ai=∏r∈Aigr,i∈[N].a_{i}=\prod_{r\in A_{i}}g_{r},\qquad i\in[N].

For any i∉Ji\notin J with |J|=t|J|=t, pairwise coprimality implies

lcm(aj:j∈J∪{i})lcm(aj:j∈J)=∏r∈Ai∖⋃j∈JAjgr≥s,\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(a_{j}:j\in J\cup\{i\})}{\operatorname{lcm}(a_{j}:j\in J)}=\prod_{r\in A_{i}\setminus\bigcup_{j\in J}A_{j}}g_{r}\geq s,

since the set in the last product is nonempty by the cover-free property. Thus (a1,…,aN)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}) is feasible. Moreover,

lcm⁡(a1,…,aN)=∏r∈⋃i=1NAigr≤Gs​(m).\operatorname{lcm}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N})=\prod_{r\in\bigcup_{i=1}^{N}A_{i}}g_{r}\leq G_{s}(m).

Taking m=mcff​(N,t)m=m_{\mathrm{cff}}(N,t) proves (30). The bound (31) follows from Theorem 6. ∎

Cover-free families are the set-system counterpart of disjunct matrices in nonadaptive group testing and are closely related to superimposed codes [28]. Porat and Rothschild [29] gave explicit tt-disjunct constructions with O⁡(t2​log⁡N)O(t^{2}\log N) rows. In particular, for fixed tt,

mcff​(N,t)=Ot​(log⁡N).m_{\mathrm{cff}}(N,t)=O_{t}(\log N). (32)
Theorem 10.

Fix a prime power qq and integers 3≤k<d3\leq k<d. Put s=d+1−ks=d+1-k and let n→∞n\to\infty. There is a constant Cd>0C_{d}>0 depending only on dd such that

(d−3log⁡2+o⁡(1))​log​n​log⁡log⁡n≤log⁡ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≤(Cd+o⁡(1))​log​n​log⁡log⁡n.\left(\frac{d-3}{\log 2}+o(1)\right)\log n\log\log n\leq\log\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\leq(C_{d}+o(1))\log n\log\log n. (33)

In particular,

log⁡ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=Θk,d​(log⁡n​log⁡log⁡n).\log\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=\Theta_{k,d}(\log n\log\log n).
Proof.

For the lower bound, consider any RS code satisfying the repair requirement. Fix three distinct anchors a,b,c∈Ωa,b,c\in\Omega, write the remaining evaluation points as ω1,…,ωn−3\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{n-3}, and let ϕ\phi be the projective normalization from Lemma 3. Put

xi=ϕ(ωi),ei=[F(xi):F],t=d−3.x_{i}=\phi(\omega_{i}),\qquad e_{i}=[F(x_{i}):F],\qquad t=d-3.

For any i∈[n−3]i\in[n-3] and any tt-subset J⊆[n−3]∖{i}J\subseteq[n-3]\setminus\{i\}, choose the helper set

H={a,b,c}∪{ωj:j∈J}.H=\{a,b,c\}\cup\{\omega_{j}:j\in J\}.

By Lemma 3 and the finite-field degree formula,

ℛF(H)=F(xj:j∈J),ℛF(H∪{ωi})=F(xi,xj:j∈J).\mathscr{R}_{F}(H)=F(x_{j}:j\in J),\qquad\mathscr{R}_{F}(H\cup\{\omega_{i}\})=F(x_{i},x_{j}:j\in J).

Hence Proposition 3 gives

lcm(ej:j∈J∪{i})lcm(ej:j∈J)=[ℛF(H∪{ωi}):ℛF(H)]≥s.\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(e_{j}:j\in J\cup\{i\})}{\operatorname{lcm}(e_{j}:j\in J)}=[\mathscr{R}_{F}(H\cup\{\omega_{i}\}):\mathscr{R}_{F}(H)]\geq s.

Thus (e1,…,en−3)(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n-3}) is a feasible (n−3,d−3,s)(n-3,d-3,s)-tuple. The three-anchor identity also gives

M:=lcm(e1,…,en−3)=[ℛF(Ω):F]∣ℓs,M:=\operatorname{lcm}(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n-3})=[\mathscr{R}_{F}(\Omega):F]\mid\frac{\ell}{s},

where the divisibility is from Proposition 3. Applying Lemma 11 yields

ℓ≥s​M≥s​𝔇​(Xn),Xn:=∑r=0d−3(n−3r).\ell\geq sM\geq s\mathfrak{D}(X_{n}),\qquad X_{n}:=\sum_{r=0}^{d-3}\binom{n-3}{r}.

Since dd is fixed,

Xn=(1(d−3)!+o⁡(1))​nd−3,X_{n}=\left(\frac{1}{(d-3)!}+o(1)\right)n^{d-3},

so that

log⁡Xn=(d−3)​log​n+O⁡(1),log⁡log⁡Xn=(1+o⁡(1))​log​log⁡n.\log X_{n}=(d-3)\log n+O(1),\qquad\log\log X_{n}=(1+o(1))\log\log n.

By Lemma 12,

log⁡𝔇⁡(Xn)=(d−3log⁡2+o⁡(1))​log⁡n​log⁡log⁡n.\log\mathfrak{D}(X_{n})=\left(\frac{d-3}{\log 2}+o(1)\right)\log n\log\log n.

This proves the lower bound in (33).

For the upper bound, (32) ensures the existence of a constant Cd>0C_{d}>0 for which mcff​(n,d)≤Cd​log⁡nm_{\mathrm{cff}}(n,d)\leq C_{d}\log n for all sufficiently large nn. Set mn=⌈Cd​log⁡n⌉m_{n}=\lceil C_{d}\log n\rceil. The function Gs​(m)G_{s}(m) is increasing: deleting one factor from a minimizing (m+1)(m+1)-tuple shows that Gs​(m+1)≥s​Gs​(m)G_{s}(m+1)\geq sG_{s}(m). Therefore, by Lemma 13,

ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≤s​Gs​(mcff​(n,d))≤s​Gs​(mn).\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\leq sG_{s}(m_{\mathrm{cff}}(n,d))\leq sG_{s}(m_{n}).

Since ss is fixed and mn=(Cd+o⁡(1))​log⁡nm_{n}=(C_{d}+o(1))\log n, Corollary 4 yields

log⁡ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≤(Cd+o⁡(1))​log⁡n​log⁡log⁡n.\log\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\leq(C_{d}+o(1))\log n\log\log n.

This proves the upper bound. ∎

The order of log⁡ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)\log\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q) is thus determined for fixed kk and dd; the optimal leading constant remains open.

VI Conclusion

In this paper, we studied the minimum subpacketization of Reed-Solomon codes admitting cut-set-optimal exact FF-linear repair of every coordinate from any dd helper nodes. By translating the repair requirements into degree constraints on cross-ratio fields and combining the resulting lower bounds with a basis-transformation construction, we established

ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=s​Δs​(n,d)=s​Gs​(n)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=s\Delta_{s}(n,d)=sG_{s}(n)

whenever d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1). In particular, this determines the minimum subpacketization in the full-helper case d=n−1d=n-1 with 3≤k<n−13\leq k<n-1, resolving the corresponding exact linear-repair case of Open Problem 20 of Ramkumar et al. [23, Open Problem 20]. We also obtained explicit formulas for Gs​(n)G_{s}(n) and determined the asymptotic order of log⁡ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)\log\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q) for fixed kk and dd.

The expression s​Gs​(n)sG_{s}(n), however, is not valid for all parameters. The affine-plane construction in Appendix B provides admissible parameters for which

ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≤s​Δs​(n,d)<s​Gs​(n).\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\leq s\Delta_{s}(n,d)<sG_{s}(n).

Thus, although s​Gs​(n)sG_{s}(n) is exact in the range above, s​Δs​(n,d)s\Delta_{s}(n,d) is the natural candidate for a general formula. This motivates the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1.

For every prime power qq and all integers 3≤k<d≤n−13\leq k<d\leq n-1, with s=d+1−ks=d+1-k,

ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=s​Δs​(n,d).\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=s\Delta_{s}(n,d).

Our main result proves this conjecture whenever d⁡(d+2)≥4​(n+1)d(d+2)\geq 4(n+1). Since the matching upper bound holds for all admissible parameters, it remains to establish ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≥s​Δs​(n,d)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\geq s\Delta_{s}(n,d) outside this range.

Appendix B Strict Inequality Between Δs​(n,d)\Delta_{s}(n,d) and Gs​(n)G_{s}(n)

An affine-plane construction yields feasible degree tuples with Δs​(n,d)<Gs​(n)\Delta_{s}(n,d)<G_{s}(n) for a family of parameters. Together with Theorem 6, this shows that ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)=s​Gs​(n)\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)=sG_{s}(n) is not valid for all admissible parameters.

Proposition 5.

Let T≥2T\geq 2 be a prime power, and let n,d,sn,d,s be integers with

n≥T2+1,1≤d≤T−1,s≥2.n\geq T^{2}+1,\qquad 1\leq d\leq T-1,\qquad s\geq 2.

Put v=max⁡{T2,n−T}v=\max\{T^{2},n-T\}. Then

Δs​(n,d)≤Gs​(v)≤s−(n−v)​Gs​(n)<Gs​(n).\Delta_{s}(n,d)\leq G_{s}(v)\leq s^{-(n-v)}G_{s}(n)<G_{s}(n). (36)

If additionally 4≤d≤T−14\leq d\leq T-1 and 2≤s≤d−22\leq s\leq d-2, then, with k=d+1−sk=d+1-s, for every prime power qq,

ℓmin​(n,k,d,q)≤s​Δs​(n,d)<s​Gs​(n).\ell_{\min}(n,k,d;q)\leq s\Delta_{s}(n,d)<sG_{s}(n). (37)

Here TT need not be related to the repair base-field size qq.

Proof.

In the affine plane 𝔽T2\mathbb{F}_{T}^{2}, consider the T2T^{2} nonvertical lines

La,b={(x,a​x+b):x∈𝔽T},a,b∈𝔽T,L_{a,b}=\{(x,ax+b):x\in\mathbb{F}_{T}\},\qquad a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{T},

and the TT vertical lines

Vc={(c,y):y∈𝔽T},c∈𝔽T.V_{c}=\{(c,y):y\in\mathbb{F}_{T}\},\qquad c\in\mathbb{F}_{T}.

Each line has TT points, and two distinct lines meet in at most one point.

Put h=min⁡{T,n−T2}h=\min\{T,n-T^{2}\} and z=n−T2−hz=n-T^{2}-h. Take all T2T^{2} nonvertical lines, any hh vertical lines, and zz singleton sets on distinct new points outside 𝔽T2\mathbb{F}_{T}^{2}. These sets form a family 𝒜\mathcal{A} of exactly T2+h+z=nT^{2}+h+z=n members. Since the nonvertical lines cover 𝔽T2\mathbb{F}_{T}^{2}, the ground set 𝒰=⋃A∈𝒜A\mathcal{U}=\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal{A}}A satisfies

|𝒰|=T2+z=n−h=max⁡{T2,n−T}=v.|\mathcal{U}|=T^{2}+z=n-h=\max\{T^{2},n-T\}=v.

For each line A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}, any dd other members cover at most d<Td<T of its points. Each singleton contains a point belonging to no other member. Hence, for every A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A} and every ℋ⊆𝒜∖{A}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{A}\setminus\{A\} with |ℋ|=d|\mathcal{H}|=d,

A∖⋃B∈ℋB≠∅.A\setminus\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{H}}B\neq\varnothing.

Choose pairwise coprime integers γu≥s\gamma_{u}\geq s (u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}) with ∏u∈𝒰γu=Gs​(v)\prod_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\gamma_{u}=G_{s}(v), and define

aA=∏u∈Aγu(A∈𝒜).a_{A}=\prod_{u\in A}\gamma_{u}\qquad(A\in\mathcal{A}).

Since the weights are pairwise coprime, the least common multiple over any subfamily equals the product of the weights on its union. Thus

lcm(aB:B∈ℋ∪{A})lcm(aB:B∈ℋ)=∏u∈A∖⋃B∈ℋBγu≥s.\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(a_{B}:B\in\mathcal{H}\cup\{A\})}{\operatorname{lcm}(a_{B}:B\in\mathcal{H})}=\prod_{u\in A\setminus\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{H}}B}\gamma_{u}\geq s.

Therefore (aA)A∈𝒜(a_{A})_{A\in\mathcal{A}} is feasible for (n,d,s)(n,d,s). Because 𝒜\mathcal{A} covers 𝒰\mathcal{U},

Δs(n,d)≤lcm(aA:A∈𝒜)=∏u∈𝒰γu=Gs(v).\Delta_{s}(n,d)\leq\operatorname{lcm}(a_{A}:A\in\mathcal{A})=\prod_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\gamma_{u}=G_{s}(v).

In a minimizing tuple for Gs​(n)G_{s}(n), any vv entries have product at least Gs​(v)G_{s}(v), while each remaining entry is at least ss. Consequently,

Gs​(n)≥sn−v​Gs​(v).G_{s}(n)\geq s^{n-v}G_{s}(v).

Since n−v=h≥1n-v=h\geq 1 and s≥2s\geq 2, we have s−(n−v)<1s^{-(n-v)}<1. This proves (36).

Under the additional assumptions, 3≤k=d+1−s≤d−13\leq k=d+1-s\leq d-1 and d≤T−1<nd\leq T-1<n. The coding bound then follows from Theorem 6. ∎

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
